speechtext:
On the orders of the day: ,
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): As a private member of this honourable house I rise to a question of privilege for the safeguarding of the rights of parliament.
I hold in my hand Votes and Proceedings No. 92, Friday, June 18, 1943. On the first page there is a letter dated Buckingham Palace, June 8, 1943, and signed A. H. L. Hardinge, [DOT] private secretary to His Majesty. The first paragraph reads:
Dear Mr. Speaker,-The King has received from the High Commissioner for Canada a copy of the resolution adopted by the House of Commons of Canada on the occasion of the official celebration of his birthday.
Privilege-Mr. Pouliot

The High Commissioner for Great Britain in Canada is not a channel of communication, and should not be, between our parliament and His Majesty the King. The only channel of communication is His Excellency the Governor General. As the letter from the king's secretary was sent direct to you, Mr. Speaker, I do not see why in the world our resolution was conveyed to His Majesty by the High Commissioner for Great Britain in Canada. It shows once more that Canada is falling to the rank of a colony. If His Majesty is part of our constitutional system the High Commissioner for Great Britain is not. I hope therefore that in future such communications will be sent either direct to one of the secretaries of His Majesty or through the channel of His Excellency the Governor General, who is the viceroy of His Majesty in Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT CHANNEL OF COMMUNICATION WITH HIS MAJESTY THE XING
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend must have mistaken the High Commissioner to whom reference is made. The communication, as I understand, was sent to His Majesty through the High Commissioner for Canada in Great Britain, Mr. Massey, and not through the High Commissioner for the United Kingdom in Canada. That is a method of communication which has been followed at times in the past and will be followed in the future.
There are two methods of communicating with His Majesty the King. One method I have just mentioned, through our High Commissioner in Great Britain. That was the method which as a matter of fact was adopted at the time His Majesty was asked to proclaim a state of war existing between Canada and Germany. The communication from the government of Canada was sent to the High Commissioner to be communicated to His Majesty the King. There are other occasions on which communications are sent through His Excellency the Governor General to His Majesty the King. They may be replied to by the king through his excellency. I assume that His Majesty, in having a communication transmitted direct to the Speaker of the House of . Commons, felt that it would be an additional compliment to the house and adopted that method.

A few days ago I promised to make a statement with regard to the payment of subsidies on wood fuel. In view of the continuing seriousness of the shortage of firewood the government has decided that the period during which a subsidy will be paid on cordwood production shall be extended t'' December 31, 1943.
The original plan for meeting the wood fuel emergency, announced on March 4, called for the payment of $1 subsidy to dealers only on commercial cordwood contracted for and cut on or before June 30, 1943, and delivered to a dealer or held to his account after March 5. Under the extension, the subsidy will be paid on the same basis for cordwood cut on or before December 31.
If they have not already done so dealers in wood fuel should arrange immediately to have wood cut for their account. In addition wherever possible they should make arrangements to purchase slab wood from the sawmills. On such purchases the transportation subsidy, which was also announced on March 4, will be paid if the dealer can show that otherwise he could not obtain wood for his customers.
The transportation subsidy can also apply to cordwood cut on or before December 31, the wood fuel controller having been authorized to pay whatever proportion of the transportation costs he may deem proper. To receive the subsidy the dealer must obtain a permit from the controller before he contracts for the supplies. Both the cutting and transportation subsidies will be made available only to wood fuel dealers registered as such with the wartime prices and trade board.
No; it is paid only to registered dealers.

Are steps being taken to see that the subsidy of $1 is passed on by the dealer to the producer of the

Fuel Wood
wood, the man who handles the axe? In my country they are not getting it. I am told by those who are producing in the woods that the $1 per cord is being snapped up by the dealer or the middleman, and the producer is not getting it. That, of course, is wrong.

The man cutting wood and selling direct to the consumer gets the ceiling price for the wood. The dealer must live as *well, and the dealer also can get only the ceiling price for the wood. The purpose of the subsidy is to interest dealers in organizing cutting, and to make it possible for dealers to take part in the solution of this problem. Much of the difficulty last year arose from the fact that the dealers did not operate, because there was no margin left permitting them to do so.

I understand that when the men who have trucks apply for permits to sell wood, after they have cut it, they are compelled to deliver to a dealer, and are not able to collect the $1 subsidy. I think only a few days ago I sent the minister a letter which I had received from Prince George, British Columbia, containing a statement to that effect.
The men cannot receive the subsidy unless they are registered dealers.
They cannot get registered.
That is a matter between them and the wartime prices and trade board. If they are cutters of wood, selling direct to the trade, they are not entitled to the subsidy.
But they are compelled to sell direct to the trade because they cannot get permits. I think that is the point the hon. member for York^Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has in mind.
What about groups who have organized as self-help organizations in communities in British Columbia where they are cutting wood? Are they entitled to this $1 per cord)?
No, they are not. They are cutting wood for themselves; therefore they are not entitled to the subsidy.

May I inquire what provincial machinery exists for the administration of this policy with respect to the cutting and distribution of wood), and generally to give effect to the policy announced by the minister? What machinery is set up in each province for that purpose?

Order. This matter should not have been brought up under this order; it should have been brought up on the orders of the day. We are on the order for motions just now, and I would ask that the usual procedure be followed.

Would it be in order
at this time, Mr. Speaker, to ask a further question arising out of the statement by the Minister of Munitions and Supply in respect to wood fuel?
It has been customary to allow a question for the elucidation of reports made by ministers. But I would point out that this is not a subject of debate.

The situation in parts of northern Saskatchewan is that there is a great deal of cordwood and wood for fuel available, but the farmers and settlers are unable to finance the work required to get it out. When the matter was before the house on another occasion I suggested to the minister that some financial assistance might be given to these producers to assist them in getting out the fuel. The minister said the matter had been under advisement. I would ask him now whether a policy has been adopted under which financial advances are allowed, secured in a proper way. I feel that in this way a large amount of Wood could be made available.

The point raised by the hon. member explains exactly why we are trying to put the dealers in business. It is the duty of the dealers to finance that sort of cutting, and they are doing it, all over the country. I am sure if my hon. friend will ask for the cooperation of the dealers in his area and advise them where help is needed, he will find them ready to finance the operations.

What machinery is provided in the respective provinces to give direction to this policy? There is considerable confusion. Many letters are being written, and apparently no one knows what the regulations are. I do not know what machinery is provided under which one can ask dealers, or those wishing to cut fuel, to apply this policy.

In each city there is an office of the wartime prices and trade board. If those desiring information will apply to the nearest office of the wartime prices and trade board, they will get the information they require.

The minister said it was up to the dealers to look after the cutting of the wood. I know three

dealers in my riding who were unable to supervise the cutting of fuelwood this past winter because they could not obtain gasoline to go to their woodlots. In my constituency most of those woodlots are situated about forty miles from the city of Peterborough, and it is necessary that the wood dealers visit the lots at least once a week to pay their men and to lay out the work. Could the minister extend a little more leeway to the dealers by way of gasoline allowances?

Every man who owns an
automobile in this country on April 1 was given a book of coupons entitling him to gasoline. I cannot understand this great and acute shortage of gasoline that is so often referred to in the house.

From the minister's
previous statement I understood the subsidy was to be passed on to the producers. Do I understand the dealer is now to get the subsidy?
I think I have just explained that.

Would not the minister
reconsider his statement regarding those cutting wood labelling themselves as self-help? The term "self-help" is a misnomer so far as their efforts are concerned. They are cutting wood for those who are unable to get out and cut wood themselves. They have organized themselves to cut the wood, and they are entitled to justice just as much as those who are cutting it and expecting to make a profit out of it. They have equipment to buy, they have transportation to provide, and those expenditures are made out of their own pockets, They are as much entitled to it as those who call themselves dealers. I would point out further that I find, on reading to-day's press, that there are some who are setting themselves up as wood dealers, accepting orders and payment for orders, without any wood to fill them. I question whether they will be able to fill some of the orders, and I suggest the minister should look into the matter.
I was not very much taken with the minister's answer with respect to gasoline. Surely he must have misunderstood me.

Mr. Chairman, I spoke last evening at the request of some hon. gentlemen who had a dinner engagement. I did not want to take part in the debate; far from it. I have no quarrel whatever with the present minister, but I raised the question of manpower before the war. The government's policy on man-power and the way it has been handled is everything by fits and starts and nothing long. We have had a different policy for every province in the country. We have done nothing about the greatest problem that faces this country. We need sufficient fuel

War Appropriation-Labour
and coal to supply the needs for nine months of the year because by the middle of September, within two or three months, we will have to be opening up our fires again. Where is the coal to come from?
In 1917 we had some trouble about manpower and a coal famine in the Toronto district. There is also the question of what is non-essential and what is essential industry. You cannot solve this man-power problem with statistics and blue books. Labour is a human commodity and it has been mishandled by five or six ministers since the war began. This is not the first time I have spoken on this question. I do not know where we are going to be next fall or wfinter. Last evening the deputy leader of the Social Credit group made reference to this particular question. Next winter we are going to face one of the greatest disasters this country has ever had if we do not have fuel. People will be freezing in their homes. There is a lack of proper housing and people will not only be without homes, they will be without fires. Many of them will suffer the natural consequences.
I think I have been around the city of Toronto more than anyone else and I know what is going on. On January 6, 1940, I saw hundreds of youths trying to get into the army. It was almost sixteen degrees below zero and all some of them had on was a sweater with no coat. They were freezing outside the Toronto armouries and many of them had not a cent to buy any food. Some of the local agencies had to provide lunches for them. Only three or four years before that some of them were riding the rods all over the country looking for work, and then most of them went into the war. Is that the way to treat labour? Here we are now near the end of the fourth year of the war; compulsory selective service should have been started before the war began.
In 1937 and 1938 I proposed a national selective compulsory service ' register with survey of industry, a domesday book of every man, woman and child in the country, our man-power, our industrial power, our economic and food power and all those things. But nothing was done about it. That is what happened in the fall of 1940 and into the beginning of 1941. What happened then? The same policy-men not wanted; recruiting lagged. As I said, it was far easier to get into the Rideau club where there is a long waiting list than into the army. Last evening we were very sorry that many of our friends on the other side were not present. I do not know where the hon. gentlemen to my left were. There is no country
party in this country such as they have in Australia, but we have a fine country club, and at eleven o'clock last night I proposed that the rest of us might just as well adjourn to the country club and carry on our discussions there.
We have a so-called compulsory system. I do not blame the present minister for what has happened, because I doubt if they could have got anyone else to carry the burden he has assumed. I would like to see his estimates go through quickly. I think it would be better to follow the policy we followed two years ago in connection with the appropriation bill, that is, allow those who have objections to say a few words on general policy and then let the items go through as quickly as possible. I have great respect for the minister and his deputy and his many assistants, but I am greatly disappointed in the whole man-power problem, especially when I go into the departmental stores, the retail stores and other small stores and see what they are up against. If all this red tape and rules and other things was going to help to win the war there would not be one word of objection in this house. But with our heavy taxation and all these regulations I fail to see how this new man-power will aid either peace or war.
I should like to deal for a moment with the question of the youths of 16, 17 and 18 years of age. What is the use of sending them to cut down our tall timber? The government has needed a lot of timber since the war started for the many different platforms on labour they have had. No doubt additional timber is needed, not only in the cabinet but for the platforms which will be constructed out of the numerous impossible proposals which they have put forth across this country. They are going to try to convert high school pupils into backwoodsmen, like the brave men who opened up this country long before we had such a system. What is going to happen when they do fell the timber? Where are the transportation facilities to cut the timber or to haul it away? How are you going to get it to the cities and towns?
I can remember when ninety per cent of the homes of Toronto burned wood which was brought in by the Nipissing railroad. But conditions have changed. There are many features to this fuel problem. The wood will have to be distributed. Just try now to get ' a bit of kindling wood. That is impossible, so where are you to get the heavier wood? You could not get it last winter, so where will you get it this coming winter? There
War Appropriation-Labour

will be no wood to burn and the people will just freeze to death. And all we do is just talk about it. This is the ninety-sixth day of the session and we have done nothing but talk about a coal supply.
Two weeks ago the mining, production and distribution of coal was made a national selective industry, but nothing has been done since. We had lots of coal before the war. Some of the mines were running only half time. Toronto spent $30,009,000 on making a harbour and was able to bring in 700,000 tons of coal through the ship channel in Ashbridge's bay. If it had not been for that, I do not know what would have happened last winter. The government is going to use high school pupils. The same trouble occurred last summer. You, Mr. Chairman, have taken a great deal of interest in the secondary schools in your riding. Nobody would engage the youths last summer. Under Mr. Elliott Little's administration the school boards were [DOT]notified that these pupils were needed on the 'farms, in what they called an essential industry.
This listing of certain former essential industries as non-essential industries is just ridiculous in my opinion, and I feel I am entitled to my own opinion. I have had some experience in these matters in the city of Toronto. In Hamilton, Toronto and other centres of population in Canada many industries now listed as non-essential are essential in the opinion of those who know more about it than the bureau of statistics and the other collectors of labour information we have had during this war. Tons and tons of information listed were deposited in the archives before the present minister came into the department. They go on to refer to school teachers. I can tell you this, that the board of education returns show that 236 school teachers enlisted for the war, but only about twenty-two of them are overseas. How many of them are doing so-called war work just at home in Canada and in physical training work, and is that an essential or a non-essential industry? Others are engaged in local sports activities and similar operations which I would not consider especially valuable or essential in the winning of the war.
Our position is by no means the same as that of England. Transfers in the northern counties of England as at the time of the industrial revolution seldom involved movements of more than sixty to a hundred miles; and similarly it is all right to transfer people from Hamilton to Toronto or other limited distances; but when you start transferring people
(Mr. Church.]
from non-essential to essential industries from Vancouver to Halifax, and taking them out of industry in the cities of Ontario, which already are bled pretty well white through voluntary enlistments, it is another matter. I say to the government, do not legislate against human nature. Last evening I was referring to the bureau at 174 Spadina avenue. I got Elliott Little to open up another one on Grenville and Bay streets; overflowing with men and women and younger people for days and weeks during the heat of last September; they could get no valid information where to go or what to do. A huge bungle went on in that connection; a great number of the members of the staff could have been dispensed with. How did they get there? Many of them, I was told, were appointed on the nomination of government members of parliament; I am not blaming them for getting what they could.
In my opinion the whole programme of manpower has been a mistake from first to last. One would have no objection if this complex system assisted in the winning of the war, but that is not so; there is no equality of service, no equality of sacrifice, no attempt to get it, and it cannot be got now. The Minister of National Defence for the army has told us that this rationing of labour is only beginning. We may wait until doomsday before our manpower resources are dealt with properly and equitably under this system. I am not blaming the permanent officials; they are victims of the system; they have been asked to take up work which no human being could make a success of. I referred last night to the splendid deputy minister and the services he has carried on in other directions. But I do not believe that in the fourth year of the war we can continue as we are now doing. Agriculture has been pretty well taken care of. No small part of the high school population is now on the farms. But the first essential to-day is to win the war, and it cannot be won without soldiers. Wars are won by soldiers, sailors and airmen, they are not won on the farm. True it is that the armed forces need food and other supplies. But the government is far from adopting the practical policies of the mother country, where women have been doing far more essential work than they have been called upon to do here. In the matter of labour, farmers have received a fairly substantial allotment of man-power during the past year. I am strong for the farmers as well; I know the laborious conditions under which they carry on; but how are we going to win the war without men to fight the battles on land, on sea and in the air? The winning of the war by this indispensable means is primary; every-

War Appropriation-Labour
thing else is secondary, although agriculture from time immemorial has been an essential industry, and has been rightly so regarded.
I wish the minister all success in his work, and I do not want to be unfair to him. He has taken up a burden which I do not believe under the circumstances can be successfully discharged. Figures are all very well, but no law which runs counter to human nature can be enforced, either in Canada or in the United States. I say this as a warm friend of labour: I have been connected with labouring people all my life, and one of the things I value most is that in my public career I have always managed to retain the respect and the support of the overwhelming number of industrial workers in the province to which I belong.

Early in February I stood in my seat and related the various stages through which the Minister of Labour has passed in order that he might learn something of his fellow man, of the difficulties of the toiler and the troubles through which he passes. Since then I have been watching this young parliamentarian, and yesterday I had the great satisfaction of seeing him arrive at true parliamentary manhood. What a credit his speech of yesterday was to the Department of Labour! You will notice that he did not say "I did it," but, like the little fellow who helped to blow the organ, he said "We did it," meaning himself and his departmental workers. I was reading this morning the story of a clearheaded, vigorous reformer who sat in the gates of Jerusalem and told the citizens the things that they must do. It was not a very popular proceeding, and our friend found himself in the stocks in a dark prison. When the present Minister of Labour spoke in January last he was not held in high repute. But stage by stage since that time he has been coming to the front, and to-day I am going to show you that when I spoke of him in February it was not, as somebody said, an obituary notice which I was giving, but an introduction of something worth while to follow.
Few of the men who serve labour but find at certain stages of their lives that their work is not appreciated, and it was perhaps not surprising to learn, as we did over the radio last night, that the labour government of Australia is not popular even with its own supporters and may have to go to the country. I regretted this, because, like some other hon. members here, there and over yonder, I am greatly interested in the man who toils, not by way of something I got out of a book but from what I have derived from experience in trying to look after those who toil and who have missed their chance in life.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that labour itself is not united all over Canada. I would have to ask the Minister of Labour how many labour organizations there are in Canada, and how they love each other. I would say very kindly to labour: if you are going to speak to the Minister of Labour in this house, speak with one voice, drown your difficulties, follow the master workman and begin to practise the golden rule; then you will find that labour in Canada will go places not only in its own interests but for the good of industry as well.
The Minister of Labour has served well, and I must say that he caught my fancy not long ago when, in imagination, whether it is true or not, I saw him, as the Prime Minister asked him "Have you any great men in labour whom you would recommend for the king's honours?" reply, "I know some great men in labour, but there is one man who stands out conspicuously in the movement, a man who dedicated his life to labour and has given great services and literally worn himself out, so that while his mind is still clear his body is not able to carry him into active service." And when I found, in the list of those who were recommended, probably by the Minister of Labour, the name of Tom Moore, I said "Thank goodness the Minister of Labour is putting into the front rank men who are worthy"; and Tom Moore has his honours. Some people may say that Tom Moore has no blue blood in his veins, but I say, Mr. Chairman, that he has good red, honest blood in his veins, and is fit to associate with the cream of the land. If the Minister of Labour has done nothing else, I thank him for having put labour on the map in this way.
I was pleased to hear what the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said yesterday about the labour minister. My hon. friend has a lot of good Scotch sense and it came to the top yesterday when he said: I do not want to change labour ministers. I think he is right too. Let my hon. friend from Cape Breton South follow that up and watch the Minister of Labour, just as I too will keep my eye on him.
The Minister of Labour first came to my notice in connection with the labour camps that were established in Canada, for a temporary purpose only, by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, and I admit that they served a good purpose. But afterwards they became nests of discontent, and then it was time to put them out of business. That is when the Minister of Labour first came to my notice, and he did his part at that time and did it well. He disbanded those labour camps and saw to it that those who were confined
War Appropriation-Labour

in them were accorded the full privileges of citizenship. From that time on he was called upon to be the "trouble shooter" of the Department of Labour, which was then under the present Secretary of State.
Another of the minister's successful assignments was the organization in February, 1941, of the national joint conference board of the building and construction industry under the auspices of the national labour supply council, on which he was serving as secretary, having been appointed by the then Minister of Labour, the present Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty). This conference was constituted on the basis of equal representation of employers and employees, and functioned successfully as a national body to adjust wages and working conditions until superseded by the national war labour board. The conference was such a conspicuous success that the Ottawa Journal commented editorially on it as follows:
Unique in the history of industrial relations in Canada, and heartening, is a conference being held here in Ottawa this week. It is a gathering of representatives of workers and employers in the building and construction industry; its purpose to agree upon a way to strengthen this country's war effort.
It is not, therefore, just another conference. Here are the men sitting down together to discuss, frankly, points of friction that arise inevitably in an emergency programme and that cut across normal ideas of "rights" and "privileges"-men preparing to sink differences; to cope as best they can with unusual problems; to impose discipline for united effort towards victory.
Under the impact of war more and more men are employed on labour work than ever before in the history' of Canada, and when men are working long hours and their friends and companions are across the sea fighting for their country, their nerves are just a little on edge; they are hard to handle, and friction easily develops.
I said the other day that you know when there is a strike, but you do not know how many strikes might have been which did not develop through proper action being taken to prevent them. The Minister of Labour was appointed chairman of the industrial disputes inquiry commission, a sort of flying squadron to nip incipient labour trouble and keep the assembly lines rolling. How successful the present Minister of Labour was in his role as chairman is indicated by the fact that out of fifty-two tough disputes, involving more than 52,000 employees, which were referred to the commission, that body under his chairmanship, was directly responsible for settling twenty-three and indirectly

responsible for the adjustment of twenty-two others. In all these fifty-two disputes there was only one strike, and it was of short duration.
I know what happened in war industry at the head of the lakes. It seemed that two strikes must come there, but both these disputes were settled, and I am grateful to the Minister of Labour for not standing back and saying: It is all right,- do not bother your head, everything will come out all right. The minister did not stand back, of course. He played the man and there was no strike at the head of the lakes. The workers, I think, did not want a strike.
Here is an order in council which the Minister of Labour had passed. It is one with which I agree thoroughly, P.C.8253, which launched the policy of wage control. Here it is in the words of the order itself:
Any agreement so modified and other condition of work otherwise suspended in the interests of war production shall be fully restored on the termination of the present war.
There is not a labour man in this house who will say that if labour has given up anything to help the war effort it will not get it back, perhaps with a little interest, after the war. I would say, in the words of the old book, give it back fourfold, because the workers in the unions have not everything rosy.
I am grateful to the minister for the organization of this national war labour board. I also want to congratulate the minister on the appointment of Mr. M. M. Maclean, one of the founders of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees, as director of the industrial relations branch of the Department of Labour. There is a man, not from the head of some great legal firm, but a man from the ranks of labour who knows what labour is. If there is any labour organization in Canada that does not appreciate that sort of appointment, I wonder what labour men are thinking about. The minister fully recognizes what a man has to put up with when he is working, what he has to contend with in his mind and in his body. There is the necessity of taking care of his health, taking care of his folks and providing proper housing for his family. Of course, I admit that it would have been of advantage to have a real live clergyman on the national war labour board, a man who looks to the other side of life, and I think that is needed; for to-day we find labour organizations sometimes holding their meetings on the sabbath day. They have six days a week to work and one day to rest. They have eight hours a day to work, eight hours to play, and

War Appropriation-Labour
eight hours to sleep, and they should have brains enough to keep one day in seven for rest and to worship the Master Workman, and in that way eome back to work with a happy heart on Monday morning. I say to members of this parliament, too, that the sabbath day is no day for political meetings. I will have none of it. If they want me to speak on the sabbath day I am going to give them the same stuff that I would give my people from the pulpit, and it would do them good. The members of this house, no matter to which body they belong, should not hold political meetings on the sabbath day, and my remarks now are directed just as much to the Liberal party as to any other party. Let us keep the sabbath day as a day of rest. If you break the law, the great Law Giver will measure you up. Remember the sabbath day to keep it holy. If you do not, the punishment will be yours, and you cannot get away from it. Break the civic laws of Ottawa and the Ottawa police get after you, but their punishment is not half as sure as that of the great Law Giver.
An order was passed recently which is one more indication of the minister's consistent effort to protect the worker and to assure him of a square deal. A fine has been authorized for employers who discriminate against workers on account of union activity. The fine is $500 for each day on which such an employer fails to comply with that ministerial order.
I wish to express to the minister my appreciation of his growth. I hope he will not feel too big for his job but will remain humble; and, as I said in February, I hope he will take his cue from the best workman this world has ever known.

I have just two questions to ask the minister. First, what is the occupation that is considered most important by the national selective service for a young man who is physically fit and of military age?

If he is physically fit and of military age he should be in the armed forces unless he has a trade or calling of such a degree of essentiality that he should be left in civilian life. I say that as a result of my own personal experience in the last war. The strong men should go to war; they should be in the armed forces to defend our way of life, unless they follow a calling that is essential in the commercial, industrial or agricultural industries.

I thank the minister for his answer, but he did not meet the point I raised. My question is very simple: What is the most
important occupation for a man of military age and of physical fitness? That is the question.

I think I have answered it. If my hon. friend wants me to give advice on a trade or calling I will do so if I know the man and know the circumstances, but I say that the duty of a physically fit man is to defend his country.

I thank the minister, but the answer shows what is wrong with national selective service, and I have stated it before. There is a gradation of equality in essential industries. What is the use of putting a boy in the army if the R.C.A.S.C. trucks are empty? Therefore it is useless to discuss national selective service unless it is admitted, not only by the minister himself but by all members of the government, that agriculture, the railway industry, the lumber industry, about which we hear so much, the mining industry and fisheries are on an equal footing with the army. So long as the government considers that the first duty of a physically fit man of military age is to join the army, national selective service is doomed. It cannot work. What I say may sound strange. Just a minute ago I heard members from rural constituencies, who will support postponement for training for farmers, saying, "hear, hear", when the minister made a reply. It shows that they do not realize the importance of agriculture, they do not realize the importance of the lumber industry, they do not realize the importance of the railway business, and they do not realize the importance of mining and fisheries.
Of course, there has been a glamour around the soldier from the start. I am all for the soldier, the sailor and the airman, but on the other hand the men in the army should be protected; and what better way is there of protecting them than to keep them supplied with food and clothing and munitions? If a young man is a good tool worker and has experience and ability in that field, and if he is called to the army, his duty is not to go into the army but to a munitions plant; similarly, if there is a farmer whose farm will be closed if he joins the army he should stay on the farm.
Some progress has been made by the national selective service boards, at least in the city of Quebec-to some extent though not entirely-with regard to farmers who have done their training. But as regards farmers who are in the army for their training or who have completed part of their training, it is difficult to get them out by reason of the statement made last year by the Minister

War Appropriation-Labour

of National Defence, which was corroborated this year by the Minister of National Defence for Air. They said, "We are not having men in the army and in the air force to become farmers". That is not the question. In the army there are men who are badly needed on the farm and they cannot get out. I do not put the blame on, the minister alone; I do not put the blame on anyone. I simply want the government to understand that a farmer is just as essential in war-time as a soldier, and a railway man just as essential as both; and so long as they fail to dissipate the halo of glory that surrounds just one head we shall have trouble with national selective service. I say' that in the best possible spirit, because I have tried to have a system of national selective service put into operation from the start, before it was put into legislation.
I did not wish to speak at any length on this question but I have put my position clearly before the minister. If the Department of Labour and national selective service are just ante-rooms to national defence, with the lowest number of young men there, less than in the air force and in the navy, we shall have trouble, and the fuel and wood business will be discussed every day. We shall hear more and more about the coal business, the fisheries and so on.
I hope that the minister will not be actuated by what was described last year by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres as fear of a vote of censure from the opposition, for the establishment of conscription. What is the duty of the government? To govern is to foresee, and the trouble we have now could have been foreseen if there had, not been so much drum-beating at the wrong time. What I say now is simply for the protection of young men in any branch of the armed forces as well as for the protection of the civilian population.
I hope that members will be able to get a copy of the instructions that have been, forwarded by the government or the minister to the national selective service. There is apparently only one in which it is said that the farmer is protected; we had no such circular from the army and we cannot get it. Their orders are secret most of the time and it is impossible for us to get them, but I hope the minister will realize his duty is not only to fill requisitions from the Department of National Defence. It is a department which should see to it that everything runs smoothly in this country in war time as well as in peace time; and he will be able to 
do that so long as he does not remain subservient to his colleague the Minister of National Defence.

There are two specific matters to which I should like to make particular reference this afternoon, but before doing so there are a few comments of a general nature I should like to make. I confess that I was amazed yesterday afternoon, listening to the speech of the Minister of Labour, that during practically two hours, with the exception of a sentence or two, he found it possible almost completely to ignore matters of labour policy such as the right to organize and collective bargaining-
If I might say a word,-
although he did say the right to organize was fundamental.

I did say a word in that regard, either to the hon. member for Cape Breton South or to the hon. member for Vancouver East. I know my hon. friend wants to make a speech, and I do not care much what kind of speech he makes-
You did not like people interrupting you.
If the hon. gentleman will stand up and say what he wishes to say-

Very well. When the hon. member for Lake Centre asked the minister a perfectly simple question, which should have been answered but which has not been answered yet, the minister became rather rough with the hon. member, to the accompaniment of applause from the government benches, and refused to answer the question, saying that he did not want anyone interjecting remarks or questions while he was making a speech. Yet he is continually getting up when other hon. members are trying to make speeches. I suggest to the minister that he should remain in his seat while hon. members who want to make speeches say what they wish to say.

As one who interrupts perhaps less than any other hon. member, except those who remain silent all the time, I want to say that it has always been the custom for any minister to correct' what he thinks is a misstatement right at the time it is made.
I think hon. members generally recognize that this has been the custom in this house.

I just wanted to point out, in order to keep the record straight-

I know what you are going to say.

I just want to say it. These are not my departmental estimates, and there is no appropriation here covering the subjects about which my hon. friend is going to speak; that is all. I do not object to what he is going to say; but while I did not say much about collective bargaining, I think I said enough.

When the minister interrupted me a moment or two ago I was in the middle of a sentence and was going on to refer to the fact that the answer he has just given to this criticism was voiced also last evening to one or other of the members of this group, namely that his reason for not discussing trade union organization or collective bargaining at this time was that these matters should be discussed when we come to deal with the civil estimates of the Department of Labour. My reason for mentioning what I consider to be the significant omission in this regard is that to me the very fact that there is no place in the war estimates of the Department of Labour for the discussion of these matters indicates the failure of the government to realize the importance of trade union organization and collective bargaining in relation to war-time efficiency and morale. My point is that when we are dealing with the relationship between the Department of Labour and the war there ought to be a place for a discussion of these very important matters.
I realize that whenever we raise our voices in the midst of war for an extension of the right of trade union organization and an extension of the principle of collective bargaining, it is said in some quarters that labour is demanding a price for its cooperation in the war effort. This is said by the same people who express the view that labour should accept a truce, as it were; that it should be satisfied to maintain things as they are, and should not use the war as a means of extending its rights and privileges. That objection reveals a total misunderstanding both of the aims of organized labour and of the philosophy of trade union organization and collective bargaining. I think perhaps I can best express those aims and that philosophy by saying that in the view of those of us in this group there are two main reasons for our insistence that trade union organization and collective bargaining should be extended in time of war. The first of these reasons is that there may be
the most efficient production; that our working men and women may have the consciousness that it is their work they are doing and that, as a result of that consciousness, they will really produce to the limit of their capacity. Britain has been referred to time and again in this connection, and the references are deserved. We know that over there the principle of the effective say by labour in the conduct of the affairs of industry is an established right. We know that as a result of the voice labour has been given all down the line in Britain, we have a truly remarkable story as far as war production is concerned.
Many of the problems that are with us in this country are handled much more expeditiously in Britain than in Canada because the workers themselves are in charge of the matters in connection with which problems arise. One instance that was brought to my attention not so long ago was the problem of absenteeism, which concerns the authorities a great deal in this country. The only way we seem to be able to deal with it is by methods of law and attempts on the part of the authorities to put a stop to it if at all possible. It is my understanding that in Britain men who are guilty of unreasonable absenteeism are dealt with by their own fellow workmen through the medium of the shop organizations. As a matter of fact the way in which their fellow workmen deal with them is perhaps more severe than is the case in this country, but the result is a great deal less absenteeism there than we have here. So it is with the matter of getting people to do extra work after the regular hours in their particular line of work are over. Labour, the actual working people, are conscious of the fact, in their shops, in their organizations throughout industry, in the say they have on the various boards, and the fact that they have a labour man in the ministry of labour, that not only is it a people's war over there, but that it is a people's industry, and accordingly they are putting everything they have into it. In my view they take this attitude very largely because of the consciousness that it is their country and their work that they are carrying on, and that they control. I feel keenly that labour in this country, in asking for an extension of the right of trade union organization, the principle of collective bargaining and representation on war boards, is sincerely and genuinely seeking these things because it is deeply interested in the outcome of the war, and because it feels that if it had these things it could produce to a much greater extent and

in a much more, efficient manner than it does at present. I assert most definitely that it is not at all true to imply that labour is trying to use the war as a means of increasing its own advantage. Labour is by no means merely asking a price for its cooperation, but is genuinely interested in the best and most efficient ways of industrial production.
The second reason why labour is seeking an extension of the right of trade union pr-ganization and the principle of collective bargaining is that there may be in this country a real experience of democracy. We say again and again that out of this war there must come a wider extension of the principle of democracy. That means something more than words. It is a fact that in this country we have political democracy; while we have a few abuses in it, we have political democracy and we are proud of it. If we are going to extend democracy it means infusing that principle into certain other phases of our national life. One of the phases into which it is most important that the principle of democracy be infused is that of the relations between workers and owners of industries, and the whole conduct of industry itself. At the present time less than twenty per cent-and that figure is on the safe side-of industrial workers in Canada are organized. In other words less than twenty iper cent, so far as industry is concerned, know anything of the actual practice of the principle of democracy.
In recent months and years we have done a great deal of thinking about democracy, and I think we are coming to realize that if it means anything it means the control by the people of the things which affect their daily lives. While the people of Canada exercise considerable control over the things which affect their lives, through their right to elect their political representatives, we must face the fact that for thousands of our people, particularly those in industry, the most outstanding phase of their lives, the part of their living which is uppermost with them, is their day-to-day work. And if domocracy is to mean anything to them, it is in that day-to-day work in industry that they should have some voice and some control. If we are to get anywhere with the idea of extending democracy in the post-war world, I submit it must take place in the field of industry.
May I make it perfectly clear that my references to the post-war world do not mean that we can wait until the war is over to achieve this experience of democracy on the part of industrial workers. If we are to have any real faith that this is a war for democracy, 
and if our people are to have any real faith in the democratic process itself, I suggest that now, when they are hard at work in industry, working in a great cause, is the time that our workers should be getting this experience. We in the House of Commons who are so loyal to the ideals and principles of democracy, and who are so tremendously anxious that there shall be no set-back to democracy when the war is over, should be most keen to see to it that our people, our workers-the same is true of our farmers-should have actual experience in the control of the things which affect their daily lives.
Because of the sacrifices involved in the present war our workers have been doing a great deal of thinking. They are working hard. Those in industry have their sons and brothers in the armed forces. They are not in two different groups at all; they are all intermingled in our society. And as they do the things which the sacrifices of this war demand, they are realizing more and more that if it is democracy we are fighting for we ought to 'be getting some experience in it now. We ought to be having an experience which will increase our faith in the democratic process.
I submit that for this reason, as well as for the reason that it would be a much more efficient way of bringing about a maximum war production, our workers are on sound ground and are perfectly right in insisting upon an extension of the right of organization and the principle of collective bargaining. Just to make myself perfectly clear, perhaps I should say that when we speak of democracy in industry we have in mind two main expressions of that idea: on the one hand, trade union organization and collective bargaining, and on the other hand, labour representation on war boards and all governmental bodies which have any effective voice in the shaping of policy.
The minister said yesterday that the right to organize and the right to collective bargaining are fundmental. It is also true that in words at least these rights are recognized in P.C. 2685. Yet we know that very little progress has been made so far as trade union organization in this country is concerned. I have already referred to the fact that less than twenty per cent of our working people are organized; and our industrial workers feel-I think rightly so-that so far as the government is concerned advantage is taken of that fact. We have the encouragement of the company union plan. We have the use of one of the most deadly weapons, that of delay

War Appropriation-Labour
in dealing with applications made by trade union organizations for collective bargaining agreements or for adjustments in wages. We have now a constant use of the charge that "it is a jurisdictional dispute". I am sorry I did not take the time to look up in Hansard the number of times that phrase has been used during the present session. It is perfectly true that there have been some jurisdictional disputes, but even as we used to hear the charge of communism or agitators from the United States we now hear it said that there are jurisdictional disputes. That is the choice phrase which is used when there seems to be any labour difficulty. The other evening we heard the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) make a most reasoned statement with regard to the situation at the Toronto shipyards. I am sure it was perfectly clear to practically all hon. members that he was making a correct statement of the situation, but to our surprise the minister with whom he was dealing at the moment could not see the point at all. He simply came back and said, "No matter how you disguise it, it is still a jurisdictional dispute".
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) who spoke a short time ago, expressed the hope that some day labour might be more united than it is at the present time. I imagine that he will agree with me when I say that the same ought to be true of the profession to which he belongs. As a matter of fact there are such things as growing pains. It is no surprise to those of us who are defenders of labour and advocates of the rights of labour that there are these troubles and these difficulties, particularly when you realize that for years and years every possible means has been 'used to keep labour down. Labour is beginning to feel that it has some future, that by organizing and getting together, by exerting its weight, it may get somewhere, and it is only inevitable that there should be some difficulty and some confusion among human beings as such. What we deplore is the fact that we have a government which is committed to democratic principles, but which seems to be unable to understand the real democracy involved in the struggles of the labour movement. Instead of helping to advance the cause of labour organization and collective bargaining, it is only too ready to point out that labour is divided, that there are jurisdictional disputes, and to attempt to discredit labour as a whole. Despite these attempts, labour organization is increasing and the thinking that is going on about the real meaning of democracy is having its effect, not only among industrial workers but throughout the community as a whole. I am satisfied the day will come when we will attain the ideal sought by the hon. member for Fort William, a united labour movement expressing with one voice its desire for democratic control of the things that affect the people of this country.
I said a moment ago that in my view democracy in industry involved two things. For a few minutes I have dealt with the right to organize and collective bargaining. The other point which is important at the present time is that of labour representation. I mean effective representation on the different boards that have been set up and which have some say in government policy. When I say "effective representation" I mean representation in sufficient numbers to have some say in the decisions arrived at. Every time we bring up this matter the minister replies that there are labour representatives on all boards. I have in my possession a copy of one of the lists he prepared to prove his point, but he knows that it is minority representation throughout.
Would my hon. friend explain the minority aspect?
The representation of labour on these boards is in all cases the minority of the membership.
I would- not like to have that go unchallenged. I should like to know the boards where labour is in the minority.
I aril sorry I did not bring to my desk the file which I have. I shall get it later and deal with it then.

I do not think my hon. friend should make a statement like that without having the facts in front of him. The national selective service advisory board contains five representatives of the employers and five of the employees, and the boards of referees contain equal representation. I do not think the hon. member should say things like that when he must know that the opposite is the case.
There is a chairman in each case. The minister knows that there are many other boards on which labour has less than half the representation.
I hope my hon. friend is assuming that there is an independent chairman.

Who is appointed by the government.

When this matter was being discussed last evening the minister sought to make the point that we should not be too much concerned about getting representation on these boards because the laws of the country were really made here in parliament.
I never said anything of the kind. It may be my hon. friend's lack of knowledge of the function of trade unionism that makes him make an observation of that description.

I shall look that up and come back to it later. If my memory serves me aright, the minister said that he did not know of any country where the laws were being made outside of parliament, and the hon. member for Cape Breton South said he knew of one, this country right here. At the outset I said that there were two '.matters to which I wished to make specific reference. I am going to say at once to the minister that I shall not mind now if he interrupts me. There are two matters I should like to get straightened out. The first is the question of minimum wages and their relation to the wage-freezing orders now in existence. I have before me sessional paper 316, and upon studying it I find that this matter has been under discussion among the Department of Labour, the national war labour board, various provincial ministers of labour and the regional war labour boards, for a year or eighteen months. I find that as far back as May 26, 1942, a letter went out over the signature of the associate deputy minister, as he was at that time, Mr. A. MacNamara, addressed to the chairmen of all regional war labour boards. This letter referred to the fact that at a then recent conference at Ottawa this question had been discussed and the promise had been made that an attempt would be made to clarify the situation. The letter made further reference to a proposed order in council which accompanied it and which the chairmen of the

regional war labour boards were asked to study and to report back to Ottawa. The actual draft order in council does not appear in the sessional paper. The letter to which I have just referred says that the matter was to be treated confidentially, at least at that stage.
As I studied this sessional paper I found out that there were two ways in which this matter was being approached. On the one hand there was the possibility of amending order in council P.C. 7679. That is the order in council that deals with minimum wages, under the provisions, I believe, of the War Measures Act. The other proposal was to present a new amendment to P.C. 5963 to clarify the status of dominion and provincial minimum wage rate regulations. To try to make it a little clearer, let me say that there was on the one hand the possibility of doing something on a national basis, the fixing by order in council of minimum wage rates throughout the country. On the other hand, there was the possibility of clarifying the situation with regard to existing minimum wage rates and regulations, both dominion and provincial.
This latter phase of the matter came to a head particularly in the province of Manitoba, where the minimum wage board was anxious to amend some of its regulations and increase certain minimum wage rates in that province. Nothing having been done along the lines suggested in this sessional paper and in the documents contained in it, the Manitoba Department of Labour was advised that the changes it proposed to make in minimum wage rates could not be made because of the wage-freezing order. As I understand it, the wage-freezing order refers to basic wages. The situation is that basic wages can not be changed, certainly not without notifying all employers affected. On that ground the Manitoba minimum wage board was denied the privilege of amending the minimum wage regulations of that province.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the idea of putting a ceiling on wages should not have carried with it the possibility in some cases of making the floor the ceiling. To put it in another way, the minimum wage rates surely ought not to be regarded as basic wages. I understand that under the wagefreezing order it is possible for some employees w"ho are above the minimum to make application to the regional war labour board and in some cases to get adjustment of their wages. But for those whose wages are down on the floor there is no possibility of having an adjustment made in their minimum wage. In

It was decided to amend P.C. 5963 to clarify the status of dominion and provincial wage rates and regulations. This amendment has not yet been implemented and consequently is not tabled.
I would ask the minister whether any further progress has been made with this intention, to amend P.C. 5963 with respect to the matter to which I have been speaking. There is another matter to which I wish to refer but I shall be glad to yield now if the minister is prepared to answer that question.

When the original wage stabilization policy-not the freezing policy- was introduced at a joint meeting of all the provincial ministers of labour, or the ministers responsible for wages and hours of labour under peace-time conditions, it was felt that the regional boards and the national boards should deal with all wages within the confines of their respective jurisdictions. Afterwards some of the provinces felt that these minimum wage regulations should go back to the provinces. Fortunately or unfortunately, according to the point of view one takes-the hon. member thinks they should go back to the provinces, and there is a great deal of merit in the contention-there has never been complete agreement amongst all the partners to the original understanding, and that to some extent has delayed progress in the direction 'my hon. friend desires to see it. But he can rest assured that as a result of recent meetings of the national war labour board there may be some crystallization of viewpoints on the question of minimum wage laws in the provinces, and when the proper degree of understanding is arrived at between the provinces and the dominion perhaps the end which my hon. friend is seeking will be the decision that is made. Hours of labour and wages are, under the British North America Act, a matter of provincial jurisdiction.

I thank the minister for the statement he has made. I am glad to ' hear that there is some possibility of something being done in this matter shortly. If action is being taken in this matter by order in council along the lines of P.C. 7679, it seems to me that the federal government should seek to establish minimum wages for the entire country at rates higher than were set out in P.C. 7679. The minister has pointed out that these are matters coming within provincial jurisdiction, but as a matter of fact,
under the War Measures Act, national minimum wage rates were set up by P.C. 7679. He has pointed out that he had some difficulty with some of the provinces when any proposal was made to increase the rates set out in order in council P.C. 7679. I am sorry that the correspondence was such that it could not be included in the sessional papers to which I have referred; naturally I should have liked to know the basis of the opposition to increasing the rates from the minimum now set out.

It was not a question of opposition on rates; it was just a question of difference of opinion on jurisdiction. If my hon. friend will read that minimum wage order in council he will see that these rates are stipulated only in war production industries which come under the jurisdiction of the federal government. May I express this as a personal opinion. After all this country is a continent in extent, and the various provinces, particularly the province from which my hon. friend comes have worked out what I regard as satisfactory machinery to deal with the question of minimum wages, although possibly not as good as some would like. You have all the machinery in the other provinces where they have established the minimum wage law, and I am convinced that whether you or I like it or not, when this war is finished and the War Measures Act goes into the discard, the respective provincial governments will again demand their jurisdictional rights. I think that is inevitable. That may be in the direction in which my hon. friend is thinking. I do not know, but I assume it is, in view of the observations he made about the minimum wage laws of the province of Manitoba.

As I was about to say before I yielded to the minister at that point, on the other hand if it is impossible to get agreement on upward revision of the rates set out in P.C. 7679 or a substitute order in council; if in other words that is being left to the provincial governments at the present time, I regret very much that the government found it necessary to use the technicality to which I have referred to prevent the Manitoba minimum wage board from revising its schedules in certain cases. I have already pointed out that there is machinery for workers who are receiving pay above the minimum rates which can be used to make application to the regional war labour board to have those rates increased; but here is a class of people down at the bottom, at the floor, and their minimum rates are

The other matter I wanted to speak about is one which I raised in the house on the orders of the day on June 7, and to which the minister replied on June 9. It has to do with complaints made on the floor of the Winnipeg and district trades and labour council concerning the activities of the selective service office in Winnipeg. The complaint was that it looked as though that office was being used by certain employers who weje paying low wages, to help those employers retain their workers. The minister's reply on June 9 really did not deal with the matter as I had presented it to him. He rather pointed out that his information was that there had been no formal complaint lodged by the Winnipeg and district trades and labour council. He was quite correct in that statement. Complaint was made by members of the council at one of its regular meetings, and the executive of the council was instructed to get information on this matter. A few days later, on June 16, answers were placed on Hansard to a set of six questions dealing with this matter, asked by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MaoNicol). I should like to refer to questions 1 and 6 and the answers thereto:
. 1. Is there a priority list or classification of industries or firms for the guidance of national selective service in placing workers?
For the present I am not dealing with questions 2, 3, 4 and 5.
6. What is the order of priority?
The answers, which are given on page 3771 of Hansard, are:
1. Yes.
6. The detailed order of priority is confidential and is continually changing as the war production programme requirements vary.
The answer continues at some length. I am not going to read it all unless the minister so wishes. It starts off, "Generally speaking", and continues. The point to which I wish to take exception-and I shall be glad if the minister will give some explanation for it- is the keeping confidential of this order of priority. The result of that situation is that it certainly gives workers the chance to feel that employers are able to use selective service to keep them at low paid jobs if the employers are able to get on that confidential list. If there is no abuse in this regard it would clear the matter up if these priority listings could be made public rather than kept confidential.

I asked for a return of documents in this matter, which return was brought down as sessional paper No. 68D under date of June 16, 1943. Part of paragraph 5 of the answer of the Department of Labour is as follows:
A copy of the circular No. N.S.S. 225 is attached as exhibit 7 to this memorandum. This instruction provides that with reference to persons employed in the designated establishments, if these persons separate from their employment, they may not be given, except under exceptional circumstances, permits to take employment other than in the designated establishments they have just left. In other words they are to be redirected to the employer from whom they desire to separate. Again it should be noted that this is not a "freezing" provision because the employee is at liberty to actually serve notice of separation on his employer.
I am puzzled at the wording, of that paragraph. It strikes me as a bit of sophistry to say to a man, "You are not frozen to your job; you have the right to quit by giving seven days' notice, but when you get to the selective service office after that seven days has expired you will be given a notice to go back to the employer whom you just left, and you can get work at no other place." I am told by workers in Winnipeg that even with respect to non-war industries they have considerable difficulty in getting permits to leave one employment for another, particularly where the employment they are seeking to leave is one in which the wages paid are very low. The minister realizes quite well the suspicions aroused in them by such a situation as this. If he can set aside these sus- [DOT] picions, well and good. I suggest that one of the best ways of doing this would be to change the situation with regard to the priority listing and bring it out into the open. It strikes me that this practice of having it confidential lends itself to abuse and to the kind of suspicions that I have voiced. I want to make it clear that we are not opposed to the principle of selective service, to the government stepping in and seeing to it that people work where their abilities are most useful in the present emergency. But we deprecate, with all the power of which we are capable, any use of the principle of selective service for the purpose to which I have referred, namely, assisting employers who pay low wages to retain their employees at a time when it is difficult for them to get workers, because of the low wages they are paying.

Let me say without equivocation that national selective service is not, to my knowledge, being used to cut down wages. That is question No. 1. As to number 2, with regard to the priority schedule, that
