of course is confidential for obvious reasons. Before that decision was reached, the question was considered by the national selective service advisory board, composed of permanent officials of the respective war departments, by representative employers and employees. It was felt that the priority schedule, by its very nature, changes from day to day and that we cannot have a public debate on priority. A plant may switch from one thing to-day to another thing to-morrow, and we cannot have public hearings in the midst of that change. We have to move quickly. If you had public hearings you would be continually discussing and arguing about priority in the respective war industries of the country. I want to be perfectly frank. We found that in the placement of people through selective service offices they could be placed on the basis of that priority listing. The priority listing is the heart of selective service. What we endeavour to do is to put people in those industries where they are most essential, and when the hon. member reflects he will see the absolute necessity for the procedure that is being followed by t'he department in this very important activity under the selective services regulations.

Is it not true that other matters, such as deciding on industry generally so far as the priority list is concerned, are made public by order in council without there being any debate on the question? Why is it not possible to do the same thing here? Even if it is done by oyder in council, to which we object, these decisions could be made public.

I cannot say more than I have already said, that it is the considered judgment of all the departments of government and of the representatives of employers and employees that these lists should be confidential.

I did not find any objection to the answers given except as regards No. 5. Perhaps the minister will give the reasons for the answer to No*. 5: Were representatives of the various industries consulted? The answer was, no. I wondered why the representatives of various industries were not consulted.

On the national selective service advisory board, national organizations of employers are represented, such as the chamber of commerce, the manufacturers' association, the mining association, the construction association. They cover that field. On the labour side are the Canadian* congress of labour, the railroad trades,, the Catholic
syndicates, the .trades and labour congress of Canada, and of course the departments concerned in the production of war materials.

In taking some part in the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Labour under the war appropriation resolution, I wish first of all to indicate to the committee one or two rather important points in the background with which the minister was faced upon his assuming the office of Minister of Labour. In .part, the responsibility for the man-power problem, so far as the Minister of Labour personally is concerned, is an inheritance, though of course the responsibility in .part is his for the time during which he has administered the department.
Let me call the attention of the committee to this fact. The measure of efficiency of a nation effectively to plan in a time of war may .properly be regarded also as the yardstick by which we may measure what this nation, or for that matter other nations, may be able to do in the time of peace that will follow the cessation of hostilities. The all but unanimous decision made by this parliament on September 9, 1939, with scarcely a dissenting voice, was to. enter the struggle on the side of righteousness, freedom and liberty; and it will be interesting to recall what this parliament actually declared a.t that time. To that end I might quote some words from the speech from the throne which was adopted on that occasion by this parliament. I will read only the pertinent words bearing upon the matters which are now under discussion. These are the words which his excellency read to parliament:
My ministers are convinced that Canada is prepared to unite in a national effort to defend to the utmost the liberties and institutions which are a common heritage.
Let me emphasize and underline the word "utmost" which was used on that occasion. Reference to the Oxford dictionary shows that "utmost" means the most that we can do. In other words, on that occasion, we endorsed, and quite properly so, the government's proposal to engage in these hostilities on the basis of the utmost that this nation was actually capable of doing. I think that may properly be regarded as an endorsation of total war.
So far as I know, this parliament and members of this parliament of ours still approve and preach war-time doctrine of total war. I think there will be little disagreement among hon. members that to approach the goal of total effort, to get the maximum possible and
War Appropriation-Labour

to do our utmost, it is essential that our wartime economy should be well thought out, that plans should be carefully laid and that such plans should be diligently executed, taking the long view of things. Either parliament meant what it said in 1939, or it did not; and I want to range myself on the side of those who believe that parliament did mean what it said at that time.
We all meant it.

I am not going to enter into an argument with anyone as to who meant it or who did not. I thought I had pretty well given a blanket endorsation to everyone in this house, and I would also include the hon. member who just interrupted me. In any event, on the presumption that we meant what we said, the responsibility which has rested upon parliament and particularly upon the government to give effect to parliament's intention in entering this war has been heavy, to use the words of the government in the speech from the throne. It is not entirely sufficient that we should be able to say that we have done well or that we have done better than others. The question should be: are we living up to the undertaking we gave when we entered this struggle, and are we doing our utmost as a Canadian people? Are we doing as a government, as a parliament and as a people that which we pledged ourselves to do?
This means, of course, that there must be careful scrutiny and diligent criticism on the part of those who are not members of the government, in order to see how far that mandate has been carried out and whether or not we have taken the steps necessary to do those things to which we are committed, efficiently and properly, leaving no stone unturned. It may be that with regard to a total war effort, on some fronts total war has been waged as far as the government is concerned. It has been waged on the government's publicity front, because the government has not been modest as to its accomplishments. I am not going to take the Minister of Labour to task on this point, because I do not think he is given to being as boastful as some people might expect a cabinet minister to be. I am not referring to the Minister of Pensions and National Health either, though his guilty look betrays a great deal to me at this moment. But it seems to me that even if the opposition were in a less critical mood than it is its duty to be, our opportunities in regard to further blandishments would be extremely limited, because certainly on the publicity front total war is being waged by the government.
When we come to consider what we have done since the declaration of war there will be tMr Graydon.}
those who will say, and perhaps properly-I do not intend to enter into any argument in this regard-that much of this is water under the bridge. There may be men and women in Canada, who will say, "What is the use of crying over spilled milk?" I submit, however, that so long as the same people are carrying the pail we still have the right to go back and at least review the position in order to ascertain whether or not we have carried out our obligations in connection with our undertaking of September 9, 1939. I think it may be said quite properly that from September 9, 1939, to June, 1940, man-power was on the loose. That was a go-as-you-please period. Certain situations did develop during that period, which I need not recall for the purposes of what I desire to say this afternoon; but in June, 1940, under the pressure of most disastrous events which perhaps many members of this house would not like to recall, events which left Britain herself in the gravest danger she has faced in many generations, the Prime Minister rose in his place and urged that this parliament give him and his government certain powers under the National Resources Mobilization Act. Those powers were given; the legislation was passed perhaps as quickly as any legislation to have come before this house for a number of years.
That legislation called for a registration of our man-power; but despite the great urgency which was pleaded by the Prime Minister, the registration was not completed until August, 1940. I am not particularly raising that point now, but I mention the matter in order to indicate that, in spite of the alleged urgency of the matter, there was this lapse of time. Perhaps it might, be of interest to see what the government actually believed that registration would do.. As reported at .page 854 of Hansard for June 17, 1940, the Prime Minister said:
It will enable the government to make the most efficient use of our man-power for the varied needs of modern machine warfare.
The Minister of Agriculture, who was also in charge of the registration of man-power at that time, had this to say, as reported at page 2125 of Hansard for July 30, 1940:
That cooperation is given to the end that every available man, every product of industry and primary production and the whole credit of Canada shall be placed at the disposal of the governments of Canada and Britain to drive back the forces of Hitler and reestablish freedom in the world.
Those were worthy statements with which I do not think any single member of this house will find fault to-day. But there is some criticism which may be properly directed to the government and those in charge of affairs

War Appropriation-Labour
in connection with the realization of those objectives. As the months rolled on, from August, 1940 until March, 1942-and I believe one might properly take in that space of time-in my opinion there was not to be found in government policy a forthright desire or effort to carry out what that registration actually should have meant; because, if the registration was to be useful, so far as our man-power situation was concerned, it should have been used right away. Everyone knows that registrations made to-day are of little use to-morrow. They must be used immediately, if one wishes to obtain the greatest good from them. While it may be urged that in some respects moves were made to place in position men and women who had registered especially in respect of certain skilled operations, nevertheless I think no one in Canada would say that there was any real attempt on the basis of that registration to allocate man-power in an efficient or effective way, having regard to the conditions existing in those years.
And so the months rolled on. In March, 1942. two and a half years after the beginning of the war, paper plans-yes, paper plans-were made. I*am not going back to the speeches made when the legislation introducing national selective service was before the house. But shortly after that it appeared as though the government were really paying serious attention to the situation in regard to man-power. I say that because they created the position of director of national selective service, and to that position appointed a prominent man, one who had the confidence of a large section of the Canadian people. There are, however, many who feel that, so far as the government are concerned, Mr. Little was too good a planner for what the government had in mind. Apparently he attempted to bring his branch to a point of efficiency and dispatch, despite the lateness of the time, and other factors which must be taken into consideration in assessing what was done at that time. But he found in November, 1942, some eight months after the date of his appointment as director, that a number of things had happened, things the exact details of which are not known to many. So far as the public knew, however, Mr. Little tried to do an efficient job. I do not think the government will say he was not conscientious in his effort to perform the job given to him. I think the most the government will say is that it disagreed with the manner in which he operated. And I am not so sure that the government was altogether ready to accept the carrying out of some of the policies contained in the throne speech of September 7, 1939. Apparently Mr. Little was attempting to see
if in respect of man-power the government was prepared to do its utmost, in compliance with that undertaking of 1939.
As a matter of fact, he failed. There have been those who said that he was not a good enough politician, and that he did not understand public opinion well enough. Well, on this score one might say the worst that could be said of him was that he failed to realize that the government programme and policy had not progressed further than to the adoption of half-way measures.
I shall not deal in detail with the events which led up to Mr. Little's resignation, nor do I think there is any special point in my doing so. But I do say that one can read from the various public documents released from time to time clear evidence of a battle in progress back of the scenes, one for which the minister and the Department of Labour must accept some responsibility. That battle was perhaps a natural thing; but having regard to what was at stake, I suggest it is not quite as natural to find that it should have been allowed to run rampant.
When Mr. Little accepted the position of director of national selective service he was given the machinery of the unemployment insurance commission. But as time went on, and the order in council of September 4, 1942, was brought to light, it became clear that the unemployment insurance offices were to be finally given over to national selective service and to be used in the field of operations over which that body had control. I believe most of us realize what took place behind1 the scenes, so far as the unemployment insurance commission was concerned. They were jealous, if you like, of their position as an unemployment insurance commission, and jealous of this new body which was to be superimposed upon them, and which in their opinion at least was going to alter the picture as it applied to them.
I should like to bring one point to the attention of the committee, one which we cannot overlook, because it is understood that in the result the battle was won by the unemployment insurance commission and lost by the national selective service. That being so, I should like to read part of a letter addressed to " The Hon. Humphrey Mitchell," upon the resignation of the director of national selective service. I do not purpose reading all the letter, nor shall I read the minister's reply. Had I the time I should be glad to read more, but the part I shall read is the one in point. Neither the minister's letter, nor parts of Mr. Little's letter apply. In part, Mr. Little's letter of November 16 states:
While I have made every effort to obtain your assistance, I have not only failed to do so but
War Appropriation-Labour

have found your actions inconsistent with your word. This makes my position as director of national selective service an impossible one.
At another point in this letter Mr. Little says:
As director of national selective service I find myself carrying grave responsibilities without commensurate authority. The present situation is one of ambiguous and divided authority, which has led progressively from confusion to friction and obstructionism. The result has been virtual paralysis in the organization.
My only reason for reading this is to show the various rays of light by which we, the public, may be able to catch something of the extent and intensiveness of the difficulties behind the scenes.
When Mr. Little resigned in November and his resignation was accepted, of course the unemployment insurance commission had won the day. I want to give everyone due credit during the war-time period. I do not think any of us have any right to ascribe ulterior motives to people, no matter where they are or who they are. I do not want to do that to-day. But where their actions come in conflict with the national interest, then I think these facts must be brought out, especially when they have a direct bearing upon the effectiveness with which the whole man-power scheme or plan has been attacked and approached. When Mr. Little left his position in November, 1942, there was a feeling that many of the recommendations he had made were in line with the words of the government, even though they were not in line with all the intentions of the administration. So that we find to-day, some six months after Mr. Little retired from the public service, such things as the compulsory order of May 4, 1943, and the declaring of a state of emergency in the coal mines of Canada. We find the government and the minister's department gradually moving into the position into which they felt at one time that Mr. Little was moving. I am not suggesting it was the only reason, but that was one of the reasons why they declined to follow the particular policy at that time.
In November, 1942, the government had reached another fork in the road. Having reached that fork, they took the turn which led, shall I say, to a more delicate and more pleasant political climate. I do not intend to find any special fault with the government for taking that action, but they did fail to take the turn in the road to which the elongated finger of necessity and the elongated finger of national interest pointed. In his speech yesterday the minister painted a very

bright picture. I do not blame him for that, because he is quite capable of doing it. He said:
In my opinion, and I believe the opinion of a great majority of this house, we have the best possible man-power policy that can be devised.
Hear, hear.

I have no objection to
hon. members endorsing that if they like, but I think it can be said that there is rather violent disagreement on that particular point. There are many who do not hold the same political views as the party which I represent as leader in the house at the moment and who are not entirely satisfied with the whole man-power position. I think the minister from time to time must have noticed that various people were writing in the newspapers, people who have previously supported the government and who, I believe, still support the government. If the minister ever makes another speech of this kind, I think he might refer to the Halifax Chronicle which contains an article by a writer who is no great friend of this party, although I must confess he is quite fair-minded. I refer to Gralft Dexter, one of the leading men in the press gallery, a man who is highly respected by the government and by all. Under date of April 8, 1943, referring to selective service, he said:
There is no dispute to-day about what happened last year. None of the objectives of selective service were reached.
That was three months ago.

The minister must have worked much faster during the last three months than the government has in the last four years if he has made the progress which warrants the praise he feels he is entitled to.
I could go on and quote others who are also government supporters and who do not think the minister's plan is the best one that could be devised. I have not the clipping with me, but I can remember taking it from one of the Vancouver papers. This was an article written by another writer who has at least been friendly toward the government and who is also fair-minded. I refer to Mr. Bruce Hutchison. He described the situation in connection with national selective service in a most homey way. He said, in effect:
We are going to lock tbe door after the horse has been stolen, but we are going to do more than that. We are going to unlock the door and go out to try to find the horse that got away and coax him back into the stable with oats paid for by the taxpayers of Canada.
I wanted to put that on record because "it has a direct bearing upon the minister's

statement. He may find the majority of this house in agreement with his statement, but there are some important people in Canada, and many people generally, who do not believe that this is the best plan that can be devised. May I point out that in so far as the man-power policy for the needs of industry and of agriculture-
You might tell us something about the old horses that were used in the last war.

I am busy now, but I may see my hon. friend afterwards. We should be frank and truthful about this whole matter of meeting the needs of industry, of agriculture and of the armed forces so far as man-power is concerned. We should consider what the people across Canada are really thinking about this. We have not used the most effective scheme or plan for the best utilization of man-power in these three particular branches. We might as well be frank about it. I should like to see the minister expunge that statement of his from Hansard. He will be a bigger man if he does. He should admit that we have made mistakes -who would not make mistakes?-but this is now our new plan, and we are not going to depart from it. He should say that we are to have a national compulsory selective service in its broadest form. I should like to see the minister take that position, because then I think the public would react more readily to his statement. There is nothing worse from the minister's point of view than to try to defend the indefensible, and that is what he has been attempting to do in this particular case.
I know the minister will not mind my referring to the Winnipeg convention, nor will the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Grant) who wanted to interrupt me a few moments ago and w7ho perhaps will be more successful on another occasion. This has been put on the record before, but I wish to put it on the record again because it represents the views of a great party which has its responsibilities well in mind and which represents all classes of our people. This party unanimously endorsed the following proposal, which I submit to the minister ought to be put into effect by him and by his government:
Recognizing that the world struggle in which Canada is engaged requires a total war effort, we believe in compulsory national selective service, and that all those selected to serve in the armed forces should he available for service wherever required.
I\ leave that, because as a matter of fact we have problems with respect to the competition of various departments for men. It
is only necessary for a man to sit in the house for a time to see the position in which the government finds itself with respect to these competitive demands for man-power.
There are certain questions affecting the whole man-power front. What is the government's position with respect to industry, labour and agriculture? When I hear the Minister of Labour talking of cooperating with labour,
I really wonder whether this government has actually taken labour into its confidence and made labour a major partner in the war effort. Industry and agriculture are our two main civilian activities in connection with the war, and surely there is no reason why labour and the farmer should not be made major partners in our war effort. To hear the Minister of Labour talk, one would think that had been done, but what are the facts? On the general advisory board for national selective service there is but one farmer. That is not good enough. The people engaged in agriculture in Canada will not be satisfied with that.
The minister speaks of the representation of labour on various boards, but I was astounded to hear an answer he gave to an hon. member to my left. The Minister of Labour said: Of course, labour has equal representation in labour matters. But, Mr. Chairman, I see no reason why labour should not have majority representation in labour matters because they are not given sufficient representation with respect to any other matters in Canada.
I did not say that.

I am not very good sometimes at remembering a man's actual words, but I was not trying to misquote the minister. I am quite prepared to accept any statement the minister might wish to make by way of correction. I was saying, Mr. Chairman, that labour and agriculture have not been brought into this war effort in the way they deserve to be represented.
When the former director of national selective service, Mr. Elliott Little, was attempting to put through compulsory labour orders he had the backing and support of labour generally in this country, and I will tell you why, and why labour was so concerned over his departure from that office. He had the backing and support of labour because he took labour into his confidence as director of national selective service. You cannot ask labour to move, to shift their position, to suffer every inconvenience unless the government, yes and the director of national selective service, are prepared to cooperate and work with the representatives of the great body of labour in this country. That is the
War Appropriation-Labour

solution, and that is one of the reasons why the Little way was so popular with labour in this country.
We hear much about the compulsory aspects of the man-power problem. But when the wartime prices and trade board was set up and when the anti-inflationary price ceiling and wage freezing policies were enunciated by the government and adopted by parliament, surely it must have been apparent to every member of the house that with compulsion applied to prices and compulsion applied to wages, an important leg of Donald Gordon's stool was left out, namely the compulsory power to allocate labour and man-power generally throughout Canada. When I talk about compulsory labour and man-power I talk about the kind of compulsory labour and man-power that has the backing and support of the trades union movement in this country and of our working men generally. Without that cooperation from labour, without their approval and consent, this problem becomes more acute and may perhaps become insoluble.
I want to say this, and the minister himself being a labour man knows it, that labour in every branch of our civilian activity has shown that it is prepared to do anything to help our national war effort. I defy anybody in this house to say that labour cannot be relied upon to play its part, no matter what it may be called upon to do. Labour is too loyal, too patriotic, to do otherwise. Labour, of course, does not want to be moved and jostled about unnecessarily. Nobody is asking that. But when the minister indicates that all our activities have been keyed up in a total allout war effort, one thinks of the situation in the coal fields in Canada and of the shortages that exist in many other lines. Not so very long ago, I think it was in this debate, I heard the Minister of Labour say that the shortage of man-power in Canada actually indicated the extent of our war effort. I think he had better tell the whole story. The committee is, I believe, well aware of the fact that one of the members of the minister's own department, Doctor Couper, when he was in Toronto and talking of his department as people sometimes do when they are away from home-I do not blame him, because it is one way in which we can get information just as the hon. member for Lake Centre found out yesterday-said when he was away from home and free from the overshadowing wing of the Minister of Labour, that we did not have the right men in the right place at the right time. I cannot quote his exact words because I have not them with me at the moment, but the statement has already been put on Hansard

and it was to the effect I have stated. Doctor Couper let the cat out of the bag. He told us what the trouble was with our man-power problem.
Square pegs in round holes.

My hon. friend the member for Davenport has always a better phrase than I have and I thank him for it. The minister talks about the measure and the yardstick of our man-power, but I think he will have to revise his remarks because, if there was one idea behind national selective service, it was to take out of non-essential industry and put into essential war-time activities the maximum of our man-power. The Minister of Munitions and Supply the other night, using figures rather recklessly I thought, said that between forty and fifty thousand men could be utilized in munitions industries generally, and I am not so sure but that he confined it to one particular industry.
The aircraft industry.

My hon. friend the member for Davenport helps me out again. He says that it was in the aircraft industry alone. That makes my argument all the stronger. It is all right for the Minister of Labour to say that all is well under national selective service, but I point out to him that there are industries closely allied to the furtherance of our war effort which require immediately and urgently men and women to fill vacancies in their plants. What do we find with respect to civilian activities generally? I am going to take the liberty of quoting again from one of the minister's favourite journals, the Regina Leader-Post. I do not want to hold up that newspaper as more accurate than any other, but at least it is reasonably accurate and fair, as the Minister of Mines and Resources has so often found in relation to his own affairs.
I wonder if my hon. friend always accepts what the Regina Leader-Post says.

This is the only issue I have, and if I can judge it by this article, I might be ready to accept its statements on other points. This is an article which I do not think the minister could have read when he spoke of this plan as being the best that could be devised, because Mr. Dexter again comes to the front with a headline in the Regina Leader-Post, "Disquieting Facte." I shall not go over the whole story, which is very interesting, but I wish to quote one paragraph.

He says:
Hitherto the positive side of man-power policy has been reviewed. The record shows that grave mistakes were made.
The negative side is equally disquieting. The failure of the government to use men and women effectively has meant that they have been allowed to remain at non-essential work. And the proof of this statement is to be found in the statistics on employment and sales.
He goes on to make comparisons by index numbers of employment in several industries. These, he points out, are civilian industries and not necessarily directly connected with war material production in the usual sense of the term. Take, if you like, from his article, the making of furs. Employment rose from 96-5 in 1938 to 103-9 in 1942. Increases are registered practically all along the line. In beverages of all kinds, for example, he says that employment has risen from 168-9 in 1938 to 241-9 in 1942. As regards personal trades, meaning laundries, et cetera, the figures for 1938 are 141-5, and for 1942 194-6. It may be possible for one to make deductions from these statistics which are not warranted as far as man-power is concerned', and I do not want to do so, nor do I desire to reflect on the industries just mentioned. But it must be abundantly clear that on the question of manpower the government has not carried out the undertaking and the pledge made to the people of Canada on September 9, 1939. To those who deny that the man-power policy is not a good one I would repeat that, having in mind the history of the problem and the puny efforts made to deal with it, those adjectives which 'have been applied to it in the past are applicable to it now, namely, that we have a muddled, misconducted, misconceived and mistaken policy with respect to our whole man-power problem.
The national selective service system has paid sufficient attention to the matter of the local offices. It is there that the whole heart of national selective service is to be found. We are dealing with human beings, not commodities; and, having that in mind, is the minister satisfied that the local branches of the national selective service as at present constituted are capable of carrying out the work which actually has been assigned to them?

If my hon. friend will let me say this, I think he will appreciate that in the last six months we have developed an enormous organization. These people in these selective service offices are human beings like ourselves; they are working in a virgin field, and I think they are entitled to all the credit that can be given them for what they have done in the most difficult job that has been undertaken during the present war emergency.

I do not take a back seat to the minister in paying tribute to those men and women who were brought in there at the last minute, at a time when they should have had years of training in job placements and in special analyses of work. The minister now rises in his place and asks that special consideration be given them because they are amateurs in the field. Of course, in many instances, they are amateurs; of course the minister was right in rising in his place and defending them; but my contention is that upon the government rests a heavy responsibility for the fact that they are amateurs when we are nearing the end of the fourth year of the war.
Upon the item of national selective service I want to make a few more detailed remarks and ask the minister a few questions. I wish he would explain to the committee why there were so many other resignations from national selective service after Mr. Little's own resignation. I should like to know why it is that, so far as I know, no real records have ever been kept-records which are efficient and really mean something-in the local offices. Perhaps the minister may be able to give an explanation. I hope he can. It is not sufficient to change men's jobs just on the basis of something which happens to be on a card.
If my hon. friend will tell me what he wants, I will try to get it for him. His question is a little vague.

I appreciate that it may have been. I should like the minister to bring down at the appropriate time when the national selective service estimates are on, the whole picture, by statistics and otherwise, as to the records held and how they are kept in the local offices of the national selective service all over Canada.
I intended to say something more, but in view of the lateness of the hour I shall close my remarks in a few moments. The national labour board is doing a job with respect to labour, and will shortly bring down its report. But I point out to the committee that what this board should also be doing is making a sweeping investigation into the whole inefficiency of national selective service, from top to bottom. I am amazed when I recall that the House of Commons' industrial and international labour relations committee has not sat for years. Surely the gwernment might appropriately have remitted this matter of selective service either to the war labour board or to the House of Commons committee I have mentioned, because, if ever there was the need of a sweeping inquiry, there is need of it in all aspects of national selective service,
War Appropriation-Labour

even at this late date. We owe it, I believe, to the country, because this body will be used not only during the war but with respect to the demobilization of our men, which perhaps is a more important matter than any of the things we have mentioned this afternoon.
Without delaying the committee any longer, I ask the minister to accept the suggestions I have made as not actuated by carping criticism but, rather, as presented in a spirit of goodwill. There is not a gentleman in this house, nor a lady either, who can claim a monopoly of patriotism in our effort to win the war. We may differ in methods, but we are one so far as our objectives are concerned, and I think we may all thank God for that. Therefore I ask the minister, in the light of what I have said this afternoon, to see to it that his department is brought up to a standard which is worthy of the great war effort to which this house pledged the country on September 9, 1939.

Mr. Chairman, the leader of the opposition has just concluded an able presentation of the position and platform of his party with respect to our man-power problem. Some of his remarks were a bit severe; I recall once when he referred to Canada's man-power policy and added, "if we have one", and again when he said the man-power policy was a "muddle". In the main, however, I want to compliment the hon. gentleman upon a very thoughtful, well-reasoned and rather clever exposition of a weak cause.
In the time at my disposal I wish to try to advance before the committee the other school of thought in regard to our general man-power policy. I know my hon. friend will concede at once that practically everyone in this country, and certainly all political parties, desire the maximum and most efficient mobilization of Canada's man-power in order to achieve victory. Since we are in full agreement as to the object we wish to achieve, this narrows the subject under discussion to a reasonably small problem, namely the mefcns by which the maximum mobilization of Canada's man-power can best be attained. The hon. gentleman went back into history to quite an extent in order to build up his argument, and I should like to remind him that in 1940 both major political parties were opposed to the conscription of

man-power. If my memory serves me correctly, the leader of the opposition was one of the first private members in the 1940 election to commit himself strongly on the public platform as being opposed to conscription. I do not wish to say anything more about that, because in my opinion that stand, like the greater part of my hon. friend's speech this afternoon, is now past history.
To-day we have two schools of thought. The Progressive Conservative party is pledged to a 100 per cent regimentation of man-power by way of national selective service. They believe-and they have a right to their views-rthat Canada's man-power can be more efficiently mobilized by some selective service officer telling every grown person in this country just what job he or she should do. This, of course, means nothing less than the most autocratic form of bureaucracy, to the nth degree; there is no question about that. In the light of the many statements I have heard from members of the opposition in recent weeks opposing bureaucracy, I am a little bewildered and confused as to how they harmonize those two viewpoints. I concede at once that there is a certain mentality abroad in the world-and Canada is no exception-possessed by certain people who do not consider that they are accomplishing anything unless they have a master plan and are pushing or bossing somebody around. The other school of thought, the one with which I associate myself, is this. We believe that in any freedom-loving democracy a much better war effort can be attained, and a much more efficient mobilization of man-power can be achieved, on a voluntary basis. I believe that most individuals know what they can do to further Canada's war effort better than some selective service officer in Brampton or Burlington or Oakville can know. We believe that regimentation or selective service should not come into play and should not be used until the actual need for it arises.
In the light of that belief let me discuss some of the arguments advanced by the last speaker. The first comment I wish to make is in regard to his desire for a master plan and his statement that because we have not what he terms a master plan, we have a muddle or no policy or no plan at all. In advancing that argument and believing as he does-for I know he honestly holds this belief-that the plan is the all-important thing instead of the end to be achieved, it is only natural that he should devote much of his time to criticisms with respect to the

War Appropriation-Labour
plan. He spent quite a good deal of time in discussing the resignation of one official from the department. He spent a good deal more of his 'time in referring to the fact that, as he put it, one commission had won a victory and some other commission had sustained a defeat. Then, of course, he had quite a generous display of criticism with regard to the lack of a master plan. In all charity, I suggest that my hon. friend entirely ignores the fact that a voluntary system can be a plan, and that it is the most effective plan for any freedom-loving democracy. I should like to remind the committee that year after year we have heard our war ministers forecast the man-power needs for the air force, the navy, the army, war industry and the like; and at the end of the year we have heard reports from these ministers telling us that these forecasts have been fulfilled under a voluntary plan. Just let me remind the committee that yesterday the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) told us that only a year ago, in March, 1942, the forecast was that we would require 100,000 additional workers in war-time industry. Now, with this "man-power muddle" that we had, and "no plan at all", did we raise 100,000 men for war-time industry? We increased our wartime workers not by 100,000 but by 320,000 in that period of time.
Then, coming to the armed forces, our ministers of national defence forecast that from March 1, 1942, to March 1, 1943, we would require an additional 193,000 men for the armed forces. Did we get them? We got
220,000	for the armed forces during that time. Once again the objective as forecast was more than achieved.
I should also like to remind the committee that when these forecasts were given I cannot recall any serious opposition from any member in the opposition as to the size of the forecasts. I think we al'l believed at that time that the forecasts were optimistic, and were quite as much as this country could expect to achieve in one year of war. To me the results speak much louder than words. With regard to the armed forces, by our voluntary system, in the air we have raised all the men we need, and we still have a waiting list in some departments. In the navy we have recruited all the men we can use up to date, and we have a waiting li^t that runs into thousands. In the armed forces, the field forces, we have recruited by the voluntary system all the men we need for overseas service, and in addition to that we have a good sized back-log of men taken on a compulsory basis, and trained.
These men will be available, should any unexpected emergency arise, and should they be actually required for overseas sendee we have them already trained.
In agriculture and in war-time industry it is true that we are running into shortages. That is to be expected. As this country nears its maximum war effort it is inevitable that we should run into shortages of certain supplies, and surpluses of others. In war-time industry I believe that in the main there are three branches in which we have shortages.
Let me remind the committee of the terrific expansion that has taken place in aircraft production. At the beginning of the war just over a thousand men and women were engaged in the aircraft industry. They were working in nine little plants, involving less than half a million feet of floor space. What have we to-day? We are nearing the 100,000 mark with respect to workers in aircraft production, and factory floor space is well over 5,000,000 square feet. That is a terrific expansion. I do not think too great a compliment could be paid to the director of aircraft production, everyone in that branch and everyone in the aircraft industry for the tremendous results which have been achieved.
Then, we are running into shortages in shipbuilding. And yet, look at our production figures. One speaker yesterday was more interested in the shortages of man-power in the shipbuilding industry than in the number of ships we were producing. We are also running into shortages in coal production. On the other hand we are approaching a tapering off with respect to some other types of production, and this means of necessity that there will have to be a substantial transfer of workers from the industries which are tapering off to other industries where we still have unsatisfied demands. It also means, too, that we shall have to make still further draws on woman-power.
The Minister of Labour has outlined our forecasts of requirements for the coming year, both in war-time industry and in the armed forces. He has outlined, in an extremely able address, just what steps he is taking to ensure for Canada that this man-power and woman-power will be made available to meet our requirements. At this point, notwithstanding what has closely approached ridicule from some hon, members opposite, may I pay a well-earned tribute to the Minister of Labour, and to every official in his department, from the deputy minister down to the last grade clerk in the outlying office. They have earned the well-deserved tribute of the people of
War Appropriation-Labour

Canada for the way in which they have kept man-power and woman-power supplied to industry and to the armed forces.
It is true that as we reach our maximum war effort-and by the way, Canada's war effort apparently is much more appreciated abroad than it is right here in the House of Commons-some forms of compulsory direction have become necessary. A state of national emergency has been declared in connection with our coal production. Some forms of direction and compulsion have become necessary.
At this point may I comment on the fact that the leader of the opposition is already dissatisfied with the way in which national selective service is commencing to interfere with some people's private freedom and private lives. He took pains this afternoon to remind the minister that he is dealing with "human beings," not with "commodities." Bless you, did the leader of the opposition not find out until to-day that national selective service deals with human beings, not with commodities? I have known it all along.
Wonderful I

All right; my hon. friend will have a chance to speak later on.
That is why I am opposed to any unnecessary compulsion. I believe that every man and every woman in Canada have consciences, that they want to do their utmost to help win the war, and that each one individually can best decide what contribution he or she can make to the furtherance of victory.
Then, again, we are asked why we did not have selective service years ago, the implication being, that because it has been instituted comparatively recently the officials are ill-trained and not ready for the emergency. My answer to that is this:	We did not have
national selective service in its present modified form any sooner for the very same reason that we did not have rationing sooner, and for the same reason we still have voluntary victory loans, the reason being simply that compulsion and regimentation, down to the time they were brought into force, were unnecessary. I wish also to remind my hon. friends of the fact that while we have a very much modified form of compulsory savings in the income tax field, to help finance the war, still a very large part of war financing is done on a voluntary basis. I have not heard any member in the opposition say that the financing of the war or the victory loan drives have been a "muddle", a "half-hearted effort," or no plan at all"; and yet we are carrying 
out exactly the same policy with respect to man-power as we are with respect to dollars to win the war. To my mind the freedom of the individual and his right to choose the job he wishes to choose, where he thinks he can serve best, are much more sacred than dollars and cents. I suggest that that is the reason why for well over two years in this war the government permitted every individual to get fitted into the type of work he or she could best perform.
In studying the present attitude of the opposition and trying to harmonize their protests of the day before yesterday and their great opposition to bureaucracy with their protests of to-day When they have stated that they want an autocratic bureaucracy to the nth degree with respect to man-power, the only inkling of an explanation I have been able to find is an article by Bruce Hutchison which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press *not long ago. This afternoon my hon. friend quoted from an article by this same gentleman. This article from which I intend to quote I think rather explains, if there is any possible explanation, this hot and cold position of the opposition. It is all very well for an opposition when in opposition to try to remain on both sides of the fence, but if they ever have the misfortune to get on the government benches I suggest that they will find it rather difficult to supply boiling hot ice-cream and the like. We have heard a lot about the Winnipeg convention, and it was quoted today. It is my view that the Winnipeg convention is couched in such high-flowery language that the man on the street does not understand it. Personally they have put the feed far too high in the rack for me. I think in this article by Mr. Hutchison there will be found an explanation of Mr. Bracken's interpretation of the Winnipeg convention which the man on the street can understand. I quote:
Profiting by the recent utterances of Mr. John Bracken in these parts I have prepared the following address to the electors of Saanich, where I hope some day to be elected to some high public office like the school board.
Ladies and gentlemen: In these grave times it is necessary for a public man to speak out frankly the faith that is in him and declare the policies 'by which he stands. I must tell you, therefore, that I stand unequivocally for general prosperity and a higher standard of living for everyone. For this reason I shall oppose depressions. I am a disbeliever in hard times.
I stand for the right of every man to have a job, a wife, two children, a home, a car and vigorous health. I stand for the right of every man to be insured against all the hazards of life, but I object to any deductions from his

War Appropriation-Labour
pay for these purposes. Nor should insurance be a charge on industry. To be fair, it must be financed without expense to anyone.
I stand for the right of every man to high wages. At the same time, I insist on low prices. As for inflation, I shall be frank. I am against it. But anyone except a slave of the banking system knows that, by creating more money, the state can pay higher wages without causing -any rise in prices. If the state will only have the courage to take away from the working people, through taxes, all the extra money it pays them.
I believe in the right of capital to earn a fair income on its investment, provided, of course, that the public does not have to pay it.
I favour private initiative. But on the other hand, I have an abiding faith in socialism, applied with discretion. Private initiative must be given every opportunity to expand, unmolested by the state. But the state must certainly remove the last vestige of the profit motive.
I may be called a Liberal. Or, if you prefer it, call me a Conservative. I am also a member of the C.C.F. in good standing, with strong leanings towards Social Credit, technocracy, communism, British Israelism and somnambulism. Also I am an Elk and an A.R.P. warden.
In international affairs it is my opinion we should have world peace, after this war. Speaking bluntly, I think we should seek to avoid world wars. I also deprecate famine and pestilence. I stand for collective security. But I am opposed to any reduction of Canada's sovereignty. I want a strong league of nations, but I certainly would refuse to give it any power.
Provided our own industries can be protected from the competition of cheap foreign goods, I strongly advocate a reduction in tariffs. World trade must be restored but not, of course, at the risk of importing foreign commodities.
In provincial affairs, I favour a coalition government composed of Liberals, Conservatives, members of the C.C.F. and anyone else who cares to join it, so long as I am in it.
I ask the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) to take note of this. He attended a Cooperative Commonmealth Federation convention a few days ago which passed a resolution on beer. I continue:
While I am a prohibitionist, I am not a fussy one and favour more beer for the public, at less cost.
All provincial health, education and other services should be expanded. More roads should be built. Taxes should be reduced as part of the same programme and the budget balanced. The government should take over the British Columbia electric railway company-
Will the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) please note.
-provided the management remains in private hands and is kept out of politics.
As a farmer I insist on higher prices for all farm products. But, of course, the consumer must not pay more for his food.
In all such problems I believe in long range national planning, a programme which will cover every part of the whole country. But I shall oppose to the last the centralization of authority in the government at Ottawa. What
we need is control of and regulation of our whole economic system, without bureaucracy.
Summing up my views as to the future, I should say that the future undoubtedly lies before us. Let us face that fact boldly.
That sounds like a 1935 election speech of the present Prime Minister.

Mr. Chairman, in opening my remarks this evening I should first like to pay a tribute to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) for the comprehensive and excellent address he gave us yesterday. It is no mean job for any man to deal with so many subjects in the limited time he had at his disposal. I wish to pay a sincere tribute to him for the success he has made of his department. It is all very well, and I know they are within their rights, for our hon,. friends of the opposition to adopt the attitude they have, but I think we must all be frank and admit that when one looks at the general picture there is not a person, regardless of his partisan politics, who will not admit, when he sits down and' studies the matter, that in so far as the Department of Labour is concerned, particularly since the present minister took office, it has contributed its fair share to the development of the things that had to be developed in Canada and to the welfare of our war effort as a whole. Speaking as a campaigner of forty years' experience, I sometimes sit back in amazement at some of the things our hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have to say, because I happen to have taken part in these affairs for considerably over forty years as a member and officer of a trades union movement. They seem to overlook many of the things that have been accomplished in days gone by and try to focus on the things they hope will be accomplished in the immediate present.
I happen to have come up the hard way. I am not talking because somebody wrote something in a book or because somebody else thinks it is a nice thing to say. I came up the hard way and went down into my pocket when it hurt and paid to get the things I now enjoy. I often say to myself-I have never said it here publicly before-that I wish some of our hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, whose motives I do not question for a moment, had had some of the forty years of hard battling that brought about the conditions which my organization happens to enjoy at the present time.

Give us a chance. We are not all that old.
War Appropriation-Labour

*

Probably you are not. But I think your party long before it is as old as this will change many of the policies it so strongly advocates to-day. Experience is one of the greatest teachers that anybody has. There are some things one cannot learn out of books; one has to learn them the hard way, and the hard way is, in my opinion, the way that pays dividends in the long run.
At the present time, when man-power policies are of such great consequence to our country and its war effort, it is not easy for a member to choose the particular topics to which he should address himself. As the minister's address shows, such a broad field is opened up by a consideration of his estimates that a member must make a careful selection of the items he chooses to discuss if he wishes to contribute something specific to the debate. Therefore, if I speak of some phases only of the labour department's activities and not of others, it is not that in my opinion they are not of importance but rather because consideration of time make it impossible for me to deal with them all.
It seems to me that nothing is more truly basic to a successful war production programme; nothing is more necessary for the welfare of our people, and nothing is more necessary for progress within Canada than peaceful industrial relations-a clear and satisfactory understanding between employers and their workers. Perhaps the public is sometimes to blame more than it realizes for strikes and other disturbances to industrial relations, not through any action the public causes to be taken, but on account of its complete neglect of the importance of industrial peace until a work stoppage occurs. Once a clash takes place; once employer-employee relations have passed the breaking point, the public, especially in war time, demands that something be done about it, that industrial peace be reestablished immediately. That, however, is quite late for effective action. A good deal of damage has then been done. Had public opinion been brought to bear earlier; had the cause of misunderstanding been removed in advance, no strike would have occurred; no interruption of production would have taken place, and continuing ill-feeling would have been avoided.
As a worker myself, as a member and sometimes an officer of a trades union for more than forty years, I am absolutely convinced that no strike ever occurs which could not have been avoided by men of good-will, representing employees and employers, sitting down together and settling differences in a spirit of give and take. During the period of more 
than forty years to which I have referred, I have been an employee of the Canadian Pacific Railway. As a union member, I never was called upon to vote "yes" or "no" on the question of a strike. Yet we had grievances and plenty of them. Some we got settled in our favour; others went against us. Maybe we were not always right, and I am sure that the company was sometimes wrong. But I must say this for the company as an employer: they were always agreeable to meeting us; they would always discuss grievances with us; they would explain their point of view and listen to ours. The company would give in here, and we would have to yield there. We tried to be reasonable, in order that the company would respect our views and would give in a little more readily the next time. It worked, for the company acted in a good deal the same manner. Mutual confidence was won and established. Union handling of cases was taken for granted. An excellent understanding has certainly resulted.
With a proper disposition on both sides, similar understanding can be developed in any industry. To encourage such a trend in industrial relations, the government should go all-out to support the workers' claims to collective bargaining rights. The right to join a union of his own choice; the right of workers to bargain collectively, should be corner-stones of our civil liberties, of our social arrangements. Leading employers will, I am sure, agree with this view. Those who do not should be convinced by government policy that they are wrong and must change their attitude. Advancement of the workers' recognized rights through trades union organization is the democratic way. Government policy and legislation should support it at every turn. Some leadership the government has given; I might mention the grant of bargaining rights to employees of government companies. But I wish to urge even broader action, greater support of collective bargaining as a means to industrial peace founded upon recognition of mutual rights. As evidence of the attitude of a forward looking employer on the subject of labour relations I wish to call attention to a statement recently made before the reconstruction committee of this house by Mr. W. M. Neal, vice-president of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Mr. Neal stated that his company takes for granted the settlement of working arrangements with their employees through dealing with trade unions; that he felt that organized labour through its leaders would make a big contribution to post-war developments in this country. I think anyone will agree that employees will respond to that attitude on the part of their employers will

War Appropriation-Labour
give their best and will cooperate fully. We must try to have all Canadian employers come to the same point of view.
I trust that when the national war labour board reports on industrial relations, no time will be lost in putting into effect any recommendations it may make which promise improvement for labour and management in their relations with one another, and also, if any action in the same direction which is not recommended seems called for, such action will be taken. No one can disagree with the statement that full war production as well as post-war reconstruction demand improvement *of industrial relations, removal of the causes of unrest.
To come now to man-power policies: the summary given by the minister of the steps taken in recent months is an impressive record. To say that more must be done is not to say that past policies have not been effective. I think the policy the government has pursued is the only possible one in the light of all the circumstances. An over-all plan, with all details blueprinted for the future, has a great appeal to it, I will admit, but I am not at all impressed that it would get us anywhere. Surely Germany is the example of a country with an all-out man-power plan; yet what do we find? That country has constantly to shift its plans, to get labour from Italy, from the occupied countries. Clearly Germany has man-power shortages; a blueprint did not avoid them. I subscribe to the idea that man-power policy must be a piecemeal affair in relation to the armed forces, in relation to industry-in relation to the different branches of industry. Of course, policies in regard to each section of the problem must be related to those of other phases of the problem-the forces related to industry, farming fitted in with mining and logging, and similarly with other phases. But the plan must be built up in sections, and pieced together later. It is not practical, in my opinion, to take a blank sheet of paper and draw up a broad plan to cover the whole case. I think the government has followed the wisest course, the course related to reality. Such errors as have been made are in detail, it seems to me, and many mistakes must be expected in such unusual conditions. But, generally speaking, the plans followed have given reasonably satisfactory results.
As one quite familiar with the views of Canadian workers, I believe it is necessary to say a few words on the compulsory measures to move men in industry, which have been taken lately. This is one subject which has been very much under discussion during the
last couple of days, and I should like to express my opinion as one who is not speaking from the book, but speaking from forty-two. years' experience in what makes the wheels of industry go round.
Labour shortages in wartime are bound to occur, and, at least in my opinion, no great plan for the distribution of workers can prevent them. The pressure on us to provide men and women for the armed forces, and at the same time for a stepped-up industrial organization, together with unforeseen changes, weather changes and other causes, must have their effects on the supply of workers. Then, of course, there is the question of skills, of technical training in industry; no man or woman can master overnight a trade which it takes years to learn. The consequence of this is that, as war develops, abnormal demands arise for some classes of workers; there may be people available, but they will not be people with the skills required. This has occurred in the present war; this may cause the less thoughtful to feel that the best use of our man-power is not being made, but that is not necessarily the case.
To overcome labour shortages; to cause men to shift to more important work-even if less desirable employment in some cases

the government has thought it necessary to bring in compulsory labour transfers. I consider that in doing so the government followed the only course open, and yet one must feel-and I do feel-that even in war time, when we grow used to taking orders from the government, there are dangers in this kind of compulsion. I suggest to the Minister of Labour that he give constant and careful study to the problems connected with these transfers to see that the rights of the workers are safeguarded as far as possible, that the coercion is administered in such a way that injustices will not be inflicted on those affected, and that inequalities and hardships will not exist if avoidable.
I suppose that these transfers are still in an experimental stage, that they will be studied and the system improved as time goes on. I hope this is so, and I would recommend that course to the minister. We know his problem. We need coal, farm production, lumber production and production of other types, and his is the job of getting the labour. But care should be taken to base the procedure on experience and on fundamental fairness. It seems to me that the method of placing large powers over the individual in the hands of a selective service officer has its difficulties. It must place that officer in a very difficult position at times, as, for example, in the case of these transfers. My suggestion
War Appropriation-Labour

would be that the actual transfer of a worker should be decided by a small local committee, made up of local citizens, and representing, say, labour and employees, together with some general members.
I realize that a man to be transferred may appeal to a board. But I think the whole transfer system would be put on a more secure basis, that it would earn more public support, if the transfers were first decided by local representative committees, rather than by officials. This is a suggestion I should certainly like to see considered. It would undoubtedly inspire greater confidence and should lead to more effective results.
In conclusion, one thing that has always worried me.is the rate of wages paid to grade one employees of the government. I congratulate the government upon recently deciding to increase the remuneration of these employees. In my opinion the lower paid services, grade one and grade two, should be put under the Minister of Labour. The finance department is no place to decide on the merits of these cases. Recently it has been decided, I gather from press reports, to pay $70 a month, but there is a period of waiting of eighteen months before the $70 becomes effective. Just recently a hostel has been opened here for grade one employees. My latest information in the matter is that only twenty-five have applied. These people cannot afford to live there.
In all fairness I suggest that the government should be a model employer, and if these people cannot afford to live in this hostel, which the government has spent many thousands of dollars to build, it is pretty nearly time that some of the milk of human kindness was injected into the members of the treasury board, so that when people are employed they may be given reasonable consideration. Eighteen months is a long time, and many people could starve to death in the first eighteen months of their employment by the government.

I should like to begin by expressing the opinion that it has been a pleasure to listen to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. McKinnon). He has spoken words of sense with sensibility, and he has been speaking to us on a matter on which he is well informed. That must always be a pleasure in this House of Commons.
It has already been said that in our opinion the application of the regulations concerning man-power has not been carried out with equality right across the country among different sorts and conditions of men and women. To that opinion I subscribe, and 
I wish to speak for a few moments this evening on a manifest instance of inequality in the incidence of the regulations. I mean the Doukhobors in British Columbia.
The minister is one on whom we look with a good deal of kindliness. He has inherited a task which to many would be an unenviable one. He has had to add to schemes which were in preparation before he assumed his present position. He has a different crop of difficulties with his breakfast each morning, I imagine, and to that crop I am going to add one more, namely, the Doukhobors.
The minister knows that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) and I, rep-' resenting two neighbouring constituencies inBritish Columbia, and having acquired a certain amount of knowledge with regard to these-people, have always done what we could with succeeding ministers to give what assistance we could to the minister in handling this problem which is so difficult. But I think it is quite-manifest that there has been inequality of treatment so far as the application of the-regulations is concerned.
In 1940 there was a national registration. That numbering of the people had of necessity to be spread equally over all the people, men and women, old and young, for otherwise the result would have been of little value; and yet it is within the knowledge of all who live in the neighbourhood of Doukhobors that many, many of them took no notice whatever of the registration. Although penalties were attached to those who did not register, I am not aware of any case in which a Doukhobor has been proceeded against for failing to register. A year and a half after that, there was a manpower check-up. Those in employment had to fill in certain cards and give more recent statistical information to the department. There were Doukhobors employed in southern. British Columbia in sawmills and in this industry and that. Many of them did not fill in the cards, and it was intimated to at least one sawmill owner that perhaps he should not be too stiff in his requirements but should do-all he could to assist the unregistered' Douk- hobor to answer the questions on the card, if the employer wished to continue to use him.
I am informed that in a considerable number of cases those forms were sent to the registrar with little more than the names of the men, on them, and they continued to be employed.
Then, when we came to the call-up by ages under the mobilization act, the medical notices-were sent out to Doukhobors in common with other people, and in many cases no attention, was paid to them. I am not aware of any.

War Appropriation-Labour
instance in which the regulations attaching to non-compliance were made use of with regard to Doukhobors. As a consequence, the people who live in that neighbourhood, the ordinary Canadian citizens, have seen their sons and daughters, their brothers and sisters, comply with the regulations at the time the registration was taken; they have seen them comply with the medical notices, and there have been instances when those who have chosen not to comply have been proceeded against, but I know of no instance in which action has been taken against a Doukhobor when he neglected to pay attention to the medical notice.
I am not going to weary the committee with a long, historical dissertation on this curious sect, but in a very few phrases I would remind the committee of one or two facts. This was a highly religious sect which followed agricultural pursuits in southwestern Russia. Because they conscientiously objected to military service they were accorded such treatment in their own country as to amount in their opinion to persecution. At the end of last century Canada required to expand her agricultural population and also needed labour to assist in her development. Therefore in 1898 she entered into arrangements, under an order in council, to bring some thousands of these people to Canada. There was just one proviso: that here they should be immune from military service. I do not join with those who, with wisdom after the event, say this experiment should not have been tried. It appears to me that with the facts before the Canadian government of that day it was not unreasonable to suppose that if these hardworking people should be offered liberty in a new country, there was a reasonable prospect that they would become citizens worthy of Canada.
Unfortunately they have not. They came to Canada and went to the northwest provinces, settling in that part which subsequently became the province of Saskatchewan. Very soon trouble cropped up. They were obstinate; they did not care for our laws and regulations; they desired to go their own way; and they did so to such an extent, with their nude parades and their indecent behaviour, that the council of the northwest provinces at last decided that it should be intimated to them that they must subscribe to our laws or get out. They had come with money; they had provided themselves with land and equipment; some of them were on the road to prosperity in farming. The consequence was that the majority decided that probably it would be better to give at least apparent allegiance to our laws, but a smaller number
decided that they would not do so and started to trek. Unfortunately that trek ended in southern British Columbia. The provincial government of the day also was rather taken with the notion that all these people needed was kindness, that in time their difficulties would be overcome and that they would settle down and be amenable. Unfortunately for the second time a Canadian government was wrong; for trouble cropped up; schools were burned; they harnessed their naked women to their ploughs and did all sorts of things which were not in accordance with our way of life. They have given trouble off and on ever since. In the eighteen years that I have been a member of this house I have made one or two trips annually into the Grand Forks country in my constituency, where the Doukhobors are settled. I have endeavoured to keep in close touch with those public men and official people who are able to give me authentic information with regard to these troublesome folk, and I have made use of that information in Ottawa in discussing the matter with officials here.
It should be borne in mind that the first leader of this sect, Peter Veregin, who came with them from Russia, died as the result of a bomb explosion in the day coach of the train in which he was travelling. There is no evidence, and there never will be evidence, as to who put that bomb under Peter Veregin's seat; but in the minds of the people of that neighbourhood there is not the shadow of a doubt that it was an unruly, recalcitrant member of his own band who did so. After a year or two he was followed as leader by his son, Peter Veregin the second, and despite the man's dreadful character-intemperate, bestial, a bully, a perjurer-in spite of that, these people maintained a fanatical worship of him because they believed him to be the direct descendant of God Almighty. He died a year or two ago, and he has been followed as leader by a grandson of the original Peter of whom I know little and to whom I shall not refer, other than to say that he is a young man and as yet we do not know what sway he may have over his people.
I come, then, to the present state of affairs; I am not going to tell the committee many of the incidents which have occurred throughout the years. I will admit that these people have not been as unruly in recent years as they were previously, but still they will not obey regulations, law and order. Here we are in time of war. It is our purpose to endeavour to harness all the labour of this country in order to do our utmost in the war effort.
