The minister made only passing reference to this subject in his speech; these are his
words as reported at page 2937 of Hansard:
As of May 25 last mobilization boards had postponed 4,747 men as Mennonites, Doukhobors or conscientious objectors.
Then he proceeded to describe the steps the government has taken in the treatment of conscientious objectors. What I want to ask the minister is why he treats Doukhobors differently from conscientious objectors? He described how conscientious objectors have been put into certain camps, and have been used in that way. He points out that many of thein have given their labour willingly and that good results have followed. The Doukhobors certainly object conscientiously to military service, but they should not be allowed to go scot-free simply for that reason. As a matter of fact, governments in Canada have taken a generous and lenient view of the clause in the 1898 order in council, because it does not strictly and in so many words apply that proviso to the descendants of those who originally came. Still they do conscientiously object-or at least they use that conscientious objection as a fence. It appears to me, and it most certainly appears to those I represent, that there should be equality of treatment as between their sons and young Doukhobors.
I would draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to a paragraph in a letter from a prominent business man of Grand Forks written to me last February. He writes:
It is a disgrace and an insult to our soldier men and women that something is not done with the younger generation of these people. With the crying need for labour in our forests, mines and war industries, and the existing fuel shortages, in every town and city in the country, to see these strapping young men by the hundreds loafing around, doing absolutely nothing, is enough to cause any red-blooded Canadian to wonder whether our government had any guts left at all. There is not a day in the week this winter that at least twenty-five to fifty of these young men of military age cannot be picked up in the streets of this small town of Grand Forks, and still the timeworn policy of "hands off the Doukhobors" still goes on.
Through the course of the years I have been of the opinion that time would solve this difficulty. That time might be a very long period, but judging from what had passed I was inclined to think I did see some improvement. When I was in the district last year, however, and once more had an opportunity of meeting the principal people, and discussing the Doukhobor question, I was shocked to find that these people now say that it is the young people, the young Doukhobors-those who have been through the schools-who now are inclined to say, "Oh, you do not need to
[Mr. Stirling.l
take any notice of that legislation. The government does not dare to do anything to us. We can go our own way." That is a sorry reflection on this problem. And it must be grasped more firmly than it has been grasped yet, if we are to do justice to our own Canadian people.
Upon returning from my visit last year I wrote to the minister, reporting what I had found. In my letter I made the suggestion to him that he should send an official of his department, not as a royal commissioner or anything as important as that, but just one of his officials whose opinion would be of value to the minister, and that such official should be permitted to go here and there and see the Doukhobors at their work or. at their farming, see those who on occasions employ them, see the leading people in the communities, and report to the minister so that he might have first-hand information. Some months later the minister was good enough to accede to that request, and asked the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to send in an officer. That police report is now before him, and I have a copy of it. I have gone through the report, and in my opinion it contains some very useful suggestions.
There is no doubt whatever that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the provincial police of British Columbia are well informed on this problem, and it is with their assistance that a solution may one day be found. For instance, it is suggested that in connection with the work of the selective service organization an office should be opened at Grand Forks. Hitherto the selective service office has been at Trail, which is a considerable number of miles away from this settlement of Doukhobors. They are more likely to ignore the notices they receive, unless they are able more easily to go to a local office. He also suggests that when the medical notices are sent out they should be sent in an entirely different form from that used in respect of those who are to be taken for military training. Then he suggests that in view of the fuel shortage, a condition which unfortunately is not getting any better as we go through the summer, there being a considerable quantity of mature timber in that neighbourhood it would be desirable to employ the Doukhobors in cutting fuelwood. This would be a means of reducing fire hazard, since these are mature trees. The cutting could be carried out under the guidance, and taking advantage of the experience of the provincial forestry officers. He suggests that if the opportunity to cut wood is offered to them, and they still refrain from

War Appropriation-Labour
playing their part in the game, then the minister should decide that they be put under restraint in selective service camps, where they would have to work.
These Doukhobors have been used to a certain extent in local industry, in connection with picking fruit, hoeing vegetables, cutting lumber and working in the sawmills. But there again we are met with the difficulty of inequality of treatment. On many, many occasions Doukhobors who had not registered were employed. The person who did not register, and still accepted wages, and the employer who paid the wages are both subject to penalties. Those penalties have been exacted against others, but I am not aware of their having been exacted against Doukhobors. That is another instance of inequality in the effect of these regulations.
It appears to me that the minister should discuss the question of treating these people as conscientious objectors, which they certainly are. Then, while honouring our word to their predecessors that they shall not be used for military purposes, they should be drawn in to do what work they can, so that there may be equality of treatment for all Canadians, and so that these people may no longer hang around the beer parlours and pool halls, before the eyes of the parents of those Canadian lads who have to conform to the regulations.

I appreciate the sentiments expressed by the hon. member with respect to these people who for many, many years have been the problem children of Canada. Like the hon. member, I sat in this house some years ago, at a time when he was on this side of the house, and I have a vivid recollection of two members, one a bachelor prime minister and the other a bachelor leader of the opposition, discussing the question of a parade of thousands of naked people on a back lawn on a sunny morning. I remember vividly the burst of humour that occurred in a house that was so dismal in those days of desperate depression. What the hon. member said about these people is absolutely true. They were invited here and were granted certain privileges. When he referred to the beer parlours and poolrooms some would think it is an indication that they are becoming civilized in a way they were not in the old country. Like my hon. friend I have seen quite a bit of the government of British peoples in various parts of the world. I think one reason for the success of our type of government is that we do not interfere too much with other people. We do not try to make Britishers out of Indians, and so on.
Notwithstanding the criticism offered by people who sometimes have not seen or experienced the contributions that our people have made toward the development of what are sometimes called the subject races, I believe considerable good has been accomplished. What my hon. friend has said this evening is an indication that these people will eventually become assimilated within the bosom of the Canadian family.
Not in our lifetime.
That may be quite true, but let me say to my hon. friend that his life or my life is just a heartbeat in the life of the nation.
The minister is very optimistic.

When my good friend, the hon. member for New Westminster, is pushing up the daisies there may even be a Doukhobor mayor of New Westminster. A good many of these people are now engaged in what might be considered callings of national importance,, namely, farming, logging and so on. I should like it laid to the credit of this department while I have been minister that we have got these people to cooperate more than they have in the past. We have not given up the will to do something with them, and I say that with due regard to the difficulties which have been experienced by every government since these people first came to Canada.
I remember that last year-I want to say this on another occasion-the Department of Labour received a great deal of criticism about the Japanese problem. I think in a large measure we have solved it for the time being. H my hon. friend will leave the Doukhobor problem with us for another six months, we shall see if we can get it on the rails and have 'these people play the same part that other conscientious objectors are playing at the moment in the life of this country.

I do not think the minister has touched upon the main question. I was endeavouring to put before him the inequality in treatment accorded this young Doukhobor as compared to that given a young Canadian.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech made yesterday by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), and I have since read it. If, when he made the statement that "we have the best possible man-power policy that can be devised", he meant that it was the best policy that could be improvised in the last six months after things had been allowed to drift into

War Appropriation-Labour

the position they were in, there may be some basis for the statement on the ground that it has yet to be proven. I must confess that listening to the minister I could not help thinking of the small boy who, while passing the graveyard, whistled in order to keep up his courage. The rather dogmatic assertions that were made by him were nothing more than pious hopes. It is self-evident that the policy which the government claims is the best that can be devised has only been conceived and put into effect in the last six months. That is proven by the fact that the minister asked my leader not to be too harsh on the organization, because it was a virgin one and could not be expected to iron out all the rough spots within that space of time. So far as I am concerned the old saying still stands: The proof of the pudding is in the eating. The first pudding was not very good, but I am hopeful that the second one will be better. However, I have not much hope, because most of the ingredients have been lost. It may be that this is the best plan that can be conceived now.
I should like to point out to the minister that this is the time of year when there is the least pressure as far as labour requirements are concerned. The minister quoted certain telegrams the other day with reference to the farm situation. Anyone who knows anything about farming, especially in western Canada, knows that this is the best season as far as labour is concerned. We know also that there is not the same pressure at this time in regard to the coal situation as there will be later on. People do not require coal now, but they will require it next winter. The proof of whether the policy of the government is the best that can be devised will be forthcoming at that time when a great amount of labour will be required on our western farms and coal will be required from our mines. Coal will be required to heat our homes and factories, and to run our railways and industries. When that time comes; when the maximum amount of labour is required, we shall be in a position to judge how this policy is going to work out.
The responsibility is upon the administration to see to it that the people of this country have things like coal. If there is not sufficient coal available, many phases of our war effort will bog down. We must have coal to heat our houses and as fuel for our factories. We must have it for our transportation systems. If the scheme which has been worked out does not solve that one problem, there will be many difficulties with which we shall be confronted. I am quite prepared to
 '
admit that all the responsibility does not rest upon the shoulders of the Minister of Labour. He has been minister for slightly less than a year and a half. Since the beginning of the war the responsibilities of this department have been divided with another Minister of Labour. My belief is that this is a governmental responsibility. The working out of a policy to bring about a state of affairs which will be effective as far as labour for the war effort is concerned rests squarely upon the shoulders of the government.
It seems to me that a comprehensive plan should have been worked out months ago rather than to continue on the basis that was announced by the minister and by his deputy, Mr. MacNamara, as late as last fall. They said they would continue on a voluntary basis until that system broke down, and then compulsion would be resorted to wherever necessary. It seems to me that the administration should have shown some imagination in that regard and realized that we would come to the position we are now in where compulsion must be resorted to. The fact that there is and has been for some time a difficult manpower problem; the fact that there has not been any comprehensive policy available to the people of this country, is evident from the statements and assertions of many responsible organizations and public men throughout this country. I need only refer to a few of' them, but they have been filling the newspapers for many months past. For example, the great wheat pool organization of western Canada sent a resolution to the administration last winter urging a new man-power scheme. One of the great voices of western agriculture, the Western Producer, as late as December 17 last, after the man-power problem for farmers was temporarily over, had this to say:
On the opposite page we publish material issued by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which we commend to the attention of all farmers and farmer organizations. The material shows conclusively the chaotic condition into which the question of adequate farm labour has been permitted to degenerate by the absence of a coherent enforced plan to guide the relevant authorities in maintaining agriculture as a vital part of war industry and to facilitate the production of the foodstuffs which are imperatively necessary in the war effort.
The United Farmers of Alberta, in the latter part of November of last year, had this to say as reported in the Star-Phoenix of November 25:
"If the efficiency of Canadian farmers is regarded as desirable, there has been a serious bungling in man-power policy," the executive of the United Farmers of Alberta has informed Agricultural Minister J. G. Gardiner, in a statement sent to Ottawa.

I quote further from the same statement, and this is in answer to a reference made by the minister yesterday to the farm situation in western Canada and his statement that he had no control over the weather:
Many farmers have reported at this office they could have been completely threshed at this time or sooner had there been available sufficient men skilled in handling harvesting machinery.
One of the outstanding agricultural experts of Saskatchewan, Professor E. A. Hardy of the university of Saskatchewan, on January 18 of this year said:
The major problem of the Saskatchewan farmer is not one of power or of machinery, but one of skilled farm labour, capable of operating power machinery.
Mr. Grant Dexter, writing in the Star-Phoenix of December 23 and referring to the coal situation-this was just after the appointment of the emergency coal production board-made this statement:
Uncontrolled competition for man-power between the army and essential war production has become evidenced in the appointment of this board whose task it is to avert a coal famine in 1943.
I should like to refer to the statement made by the minister as reported by the Canadian Press on November 7, 1942. I quote:
Mitchell said the way the British labour ministry's man-power activities are coordinated with production functions of supply departments on both national and regional levels impressed him deeply.
"We have been groping for procedure of the same kind and I hope I have found the key to it" said the minister.
He said that if he was able to judge what he had seen of production in visits to factories since he has been here the tempo in British plants is faster than in Canadian factories. And he added: "I shall have some wholesome things to say to Canadian employers and workmen on my return."
My leader this afternoon referred to a series of articles which was published in the western press of this country last November and December. These articles were written by Mr. Grant Dexter, who, to say the least, has been favourably inclined toward this government for a number of years and certainly has never been anything but critical of the party to which I have the honour to belong. I do not refer to these articles for the same purpose for which some of them were referred to this afternoon by the leader of the opposition. I do so for the purpose of discussing what I would call the Elliott Little case. I must confess that this matter has been on my mind for many months. From what I have been able to ascertain from a reading of the press and discussing the matter with people, some of whom purport to be in a position to know 72537-254}
or have been able to find out, it does seem to me that this man Elliott Little was given a very unfair deal by the administration.
May I say, first of all, that I do not know Mr. Little. But I do know this, that he was held in the very highest regard by the agricultural organizations of this country. I know that at the time of his resignation statements were made by the two largest labour organizations in this country, the trades and labour congress and the Canadian congress of labour, attesting to this. I want to refer to a Canadian Press dispatch of November 18, 1942. The first statement is by Percy R. Bengough, vice-president of the trades and labour congress. He stated: '
As far as Mr. Little is concerned we believe he is honest and capable. As far as the Minister of Labour is concerned we have resented his dictatorial and uncompromising attitude. Generally, labour from coast to coast does not like him.
Here is the statement of Mr. A. R. Mosher, president of the Canadian congress of labour:
The Canadian-congress of labour is very deeply disturbed by the rumour that Elliott Little, director of national selective service, has resigned from that office as a result of a controversy with the Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, Minister of Labour.
It is a matter of public knowledge that the man-power programme has bogged down, but this, in the opinion of the press, is due primarily to the lack of an adequate government policy with regard to the whole war effort.
The responsibility for the present situation rests upon the cabinet, and especially upon the Minister of Labour. Mr. Little has been handicapped from the start by the failure of the government to make up its mind about manpower, and to give him authority to carry out a definite policy.
It is just about eleven months ago that I met one of the leading labour men of my city. He had just returned from a meeting of labour men in Winnipeg which had been addressed by Mr. Elliott Little. I was very pleased that Mr. Little was in charge of this matter then., and I must confess that I was pleased to hear the praise showered on Mr. Little by this labour man for the aggressive attitude he, Mr. Little, had taken and for the impression he had given to that labour meeting in the city of Winnipeg.
In my opinion, and so far as I can ascertain, Mr. Little did not quit the ship, as was stated by the minister a few days ago. He was pushed off. He had been given a job, but had been given no authority to cany it out. In his own tyords the trouble was:
The paralysis which has overtaken selective service was, of course, a progresive development over several months and the minister was aware of outstanding difficulties before he left for

England. During his absence I prepared proposals which I had hoped would serve as a basis for a constructive solution upon his return.
His attitude then, when I pressed for serious consideration of these proposals, was such that I obviously could not expect that support from him which is necessary if this or any other plan of national selective service is to function properly. I had no alternative but to submit my immediate resignation.
I have referred to the series of articles written by Mr. Grant Dexter. Mr. Dexter has a, reputation for being an intelligent and hard working editorial writer. He is known for his diligence in ascertaining the facts, and the statements he makes in this series of articles completely exonerate Mr. Elliott Little. For example, on November 9 last he said:
When selective service was announced last March great things were expected of it. As described by Mr. King in parliament, its responsibilities -were great. But few noted at the time that its powers were strictly limited. Mr. Little and others associated with him in administering selective service took the assignment in earnest, went about the country making speeches about what was going to happen. Figuratively they were like the farmer who thinks he has much land to work, but tunes up the tractors and the gang ploughs only to discover that all he really needs is a hand trowel to cultivate a window box.
To this day, seven months after the announcement, selective service is impotent, on its own, to hire a stenographer or to pay a bill. It has no power to take men from unimportant jobs and put them to work on essential ones. It can deal with people who come to its labour offices looking for work, but no more. Great sections of the population, and therefore of manpower, are totally withdrawn from its field of action-agriculture, for example. And the areas so blocked off are increasing, not decreasing; as witness the freezing, even if only temporarily, of half a dozen basic industries a few days ago.
Most people seem to have been thinking of selective service as the agency which would coordinate the war effort. There is, however, no warrant for such a view. This may happen: the crisis may have this result.
And on November 11 in another article he wrote as follows:
Most people think of national selective service as the organization whose task it is to give to every Canadian the job he can do best in this war. Indeed these are the words used by Elliott Little, the director, in a national broadcast on April 8, 1942, some two weeks after he was appointed.
_ The record, however, proves this is a mistaken idea. The confusion which now exists is only in a minor way attributable to Mr. Little and his associates. It is the result of government policy which, it would seem, has swerved sharply since March 24. In consequence, the position wTith respect to the mobilization of man-power has become increasingly complex. Right now it is a task shared by several agencies of government.
In retrospect, the action to mobilize manpower seems to have been halting and unsure.

The explanation in part is to be found in circumstances for which Mr. Little is not responsible. His contribution to present confusion has been due only to an apparent miscalculation of the pow'ers and responsibilities of selective service.
An article to a similar effect is set forth in the Star-Phoenix of November 30, after the resignation of Mr. Little. It is practically a repetition of one of the previous articles. I will read just the latter part:
Thus selective service, after six months of confusion, vacates the field so far as coordination of man-power is concerned. The four major contestants-army, munitions and supply, agriculture and essential civilian services-remain in the battle. Each of them is represented in cabinet by a different minister.
Coordination of man-power, therefore, remains just where it w'as last March before Mr. Little w-as appointed'-a problem for the government. The moral of the Little episode is that no one man can do this job. Only the government can coordinate its competing departments.
And then it goes on, referring to the order in council which I have cited, and of which I may have something to say in a minute:
On examination the charge against Mr. Little of presenting his minister with a 70-page proposition and expecting an early answer does not stand up. The 70 pages comprise, largely, a consolidation of regulations and orders already in effect. Over 60 pages of the total are merely a re-hash of orders already approved by the government. The new material can be read in not more than 15 minutes.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have something to say in connection with this order in council, because I believe that the manner in which it was presented to the people of this country constitutes one of the most unfair things I have ever known. For example, let me point this out. This order, this draft order in council, was, at the expense of the Canadian people to the tune of $558.40, printed so that it could be sent out for the purpose of showing that Elliott Little was nothing but a dictator-9,500 copies in English and 3,500 copies in French; and particular attention-and this is the point to which I take the greatest exception - was drawn to a certain section of the draft order in council. To the ordinary person who has not studied law it sounds pretty terrible, but may I say that I do not believe Mr. Little had anything to do with the drafting of this section, and I will explain why in a minute.
Section 21, page 32 of that draft order in council, is as follows:
No person shall, in the course of an investigation under this section, insult the director or wilfully interrupt any proceeding before the director, or refuse to obey any order made by the director in the course of an investigation; and if a person does any such thing the director may, without affecting such person's liability for

War Appropriation-Labour
contravening regulations, direct any peace officer to take him into custody and remove him from the precincts and presence of the director to be detained in custody until the conclusion of the day's sitting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: What section is that?

Section 21, page 32. That section was spread all across this country in black type for the purpose of showing what kind of man Elliott Little was, and there was great chortling and glee in many sections of the Liberal party in my particular part of the country because they could pick this out and say, "What kind of man is this who does not want to be insulted and puts in a draft order in council to this effect?" This draft order in council was drawn up by members of the Department of Labour and the Department of Justice. That particular section as a matter of fact is practically the same as a section in the Combines Investigation Act of this country, which was, I understand, drawn up and was certainly passed under the supervision of the present Prime Minister of Canada. Section 33 of the Combines Investigation Act, chapter 26, revised statutes of Canada, 1927, is as follows:
If in any proceedings before the Registrar or any commissioner any person wilfully insults the Registrar or any commissioner, or wilfully interrupts the proceedings, or is guilty in any other manner of any wilful contempt in the face of the Registrar or commissioner, the Registrar or commissioner may direct any constable to take the person offending into custody and remove him from the precincts and presence of the Registrar or commissioner, to be detained in custody until the conclusion of that day's sitting.
It is practically identically the same thing that was set out in this draft order in council and which was impressed on the Canadian people as an example of what a dictator this man was; yet it is a section which has been on the statute books of this country for at least the last twenty years. That was taking a very unfair advantage of Mr. Little, and it seems to me that, if the Minister of Labour had been as fair as he states he wishes to be, he would have drawn that fact to the attention of the Canadian people.
To my mind the confusion which has been demonstrated to the people of this country by the actions of the administration in its manpower policy is proven by the fact that, during the course of the last two years, they have had not only two ministers of labour, but two ministers of national war services, and now they have called for a parliamentary assistant -to whom I wish the very best of luck, because I believe that he will need it.
I wish now to refer, before I complete my remarks, to one particular thing in connection with my own constituency. I refer to the
flour mills situation, which is very grave, and which I believe, unless it is solved, will affect many sections of Canada's war effort and will put the people of this country in grave peril.
We have in western Canada many large flour mills, and I receive, not complaints, because these are not the kind of people who complain, but numerous suggestions from them that some special consideration, should be given to the men who work in the flour mills. There is a great deal of heavy work to be done there; yet it would appear that there is no special priority so far as they are concerned; at least it is certainly not as high a priority as obtains in other cases. The matter of the manufacture of flour is very important in this country, and I submit to the minister and to the officials who are in charge of the administration of these priorities that they should see to it that the necessary heavy labour, a good deal of which is required in connection with flour mills, is available. I wish to quote from a copy of a letter which was sent to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) from one of the mills in that city, and a copy of which was sent to me by the manager of a Saskatoon firm. It states as follows:
. . . But those vital food processing industries, long established on the prairies are inexorably being forced to curtail their output or shut down altogether, because of the manpower shortage. Such a condition, at this most crucial period in our national effort, is not only intolerable, but must appear incredible. Nevertheless, it is absolutely true.
We are under present regulations, unable to help ourselves. Our rating is apparently not high enough to warrant first choice of any available labour. That, seemingly is reserved for repair depots, coal mines, or oil refineries. We consider our food industries vitally essential. We will be here long after the war is won-if we survive.
I submit that the case is an imperative one and should receive immediate consideration.
Will the hon. member tell us who wrote that?

Gladly. It was written by
Robin Hood flour mills of Moose Jaw, of which Mr. Larkins is manager.

As the representative of
an important constituency in Montreal, and representing labour, I should like to say a few words, but first I would ask the committee to be indulgent with me because I intend to speak in English and unfortunately I am not thoroughly familiar with the language. My first word will be one of congratulation to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) upon the wonderful speech he made in the house. He has given us an

War Appropriation-Labour
interesting statement of the affairs of his department, and not only to the house but to the country as well, which was very anxious to get his explanation.
At the beginning of the session there were labour troubles throughout the country and in many places people were asking for the head of the Minister of Labour. I well remember, as all hon. members no doubt do, the speech which the Prime Minister made in this house when, referring to the Minister of Labour, he said that at the time when it was decided to have a labour man in the cabinet the first thing he did was to ask Mr. Tom Moore to join the government in that capacity. Unfortunately, for some reason or another, Mr. Tom Moore refused, but he did suggest to the Prime Minister that the best man he could choose in the country was the hon. gentleman who now occupies the position of Minister of Labour.
If I rise to-night to pay my tribute to the Minister of Labour, it is because, not only in my own province and in my own constituency, but throughout Canada, those who think likewise are in very good company, since they are in the company of Mr. Tom Moore.
We have heard many criticisms of the minister since the beginning of the session, and of course we need to have criticism. It is the role of the opposition; it is the role of all parties wdio do not support the government, to criticize, and I do not blame them. The first criticism we have heard is that the Minister of Labour did not succeed in allotting to every department of our economic life sufficient man-power, and in some other quarters other critics have said that as a labour man he did not treat the labour men as he should have done. It is interesting to study the part which the Progressive Conservative party has played in the criticism of the Minister of Labour, and the part which our friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have taken. The Conservative party have taken the position of the patriot who wants to do more than anybody else to win the war and who thinks that we have not done enough, that w'e are not making an all-out war effort. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has assumed the role of the protector of the labouring classes.
I do not wish to impute motives to those hon. members. They have tried, I suppose, to do their best for their country. I realize, however, as a man who has been in politics for many years, what it would be like if there were an election. The Conservatives would go before the people and say, "The Liberal party has not done its utmost to win the war; it has not made an all-out war effort because it has
[Mr. Fauteux.l
not had conscription." And the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation would say to the people, "We are the only ones who have looked after you employees during the four years that the government has been in power."
Hon. members may recall what was said last session-and I do not like to speak about the past; I do not like to speak about measures that have been already discussed at considerable length, measures, moreover, that might create division between provinces. I think hon. members will give me credit for having done my utmost in this house to promote national unity, and perhaps they will allow me to say that, even though I am a young man, I have a son who is only eighteen years of age and who is now in the maritime provinces awaiting embarkation. In a few weeks' time he will be at sea going to defend his country, and I am proud of him.
What did we say during the last session on the question of conscription? If I refer to this subject it is because it was introduced by the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). I remember when I spoke against conscription at the last session I said to this house that I was opposed to conscription for overseas but not for service in this country, and I did so because, like many other Canadians, I believed that we should retain as many Canadians as possible in Canada to work in order to comply with Mr. Churchill's request, "Give us the tools and we will finish the job." I was sincere; we were sincere, but during that time we heard our hon. friends opposite, the Conservative party, trying to impose upon the Prime Minister and the government of this country an all-out, total war effort, which to them meant conscription. We imposed conscription for Canada; we amended the law in order to permit the government to send men overseas or anywhere by order in council, if the men were needed. I believe, knowing the Conservatives of the province of Quebec-I will not say throughout the country-that they were sorry our Prime Minister did not impose conscription for overseas; not to save our country, not to save the allies, but to save their own party. I was greatly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre when he spoke of Mr. MacNamara, as reported at page 3956 of Hansard of yesterday as follows:
My hon. friends on the government side never admit that they have brought in conscription; they do not admit that the present system is a means by which men are forced to volunteer in the armed forces for overseas service, but when the deputy minister of labour was speaking at this meeting he endeavoured to explain to those who were present why it was that Canada did not have selective service by which men would serve all over the world just as they have in the United States.

War Appropriation-Labour
Then he further quoted what Mr. MacNamara had said and followed it with these words; and I ask you, Mr. Chairman, and my hon. friends from the province of Quebec to listen to this statement, to show the sincerity of those in my province who were asking for conscription:
At last we have from the mouth of an official of the Department of Labour definite proof of what we have been endeavouring to place before the house on more than one occasion, that Canada has conscription.
That is what the Conservative party were interested in saving. I said in the beginning that I did not want to impute motives to the hon. member, but I really believe that the Conservative party in my own province were interested in having conscription, not to help Canada's cause, not to help the allied cause, but to help their party. What were we asking for last year? We did everything possible to impress upon the government that we wanted selective service in order that every Canadian should serve where he was best fitted to serve. We hear complaints now that we have not enough man-power on the farms. How many members on this side of the house have been asking the government to free farmers' sons, not from their duty, not because they were cowards and did not want to serve at the front, but because we thought at the time-and I believe we were right-that we needed those young men to serve on the home front, to serve on the farms not only of Quebec but of the whole country? I believe the best proof that we were right is to be found in the fact that this session we do not hear, as we heard last session, hon. members opposite asking the government to send all the young men possible overseas. This year they are complaining that we have not enough men in this country to serve in our war plants and on our farms.

Do you think we
have?

Just a moment, my hon. friend. My congratulations go to the man who is at the head of the country, who has been chosen as Prime Minister of this country and has served in that office for many years. He was not only chosen by Liberals, but he was chosen by all Canada. When he was accused of playing politics; when be was accused of serving his party, he was really sacrificing himself and his party to serve his country.
I said a few moments ago, Mr. Chairman, that other criticisms came from the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. They would have the working people of
Canada believe that they are the only men who will protect them. If I remember correctly, the present labour minister was not chosen because he was a Liberal; if I am not mistaken, only a few years ago he occupied a seat in the opposition side of this house when the Liberals were in power. He was chosen as labour minister because he was a labour man, because he was an able man and because he was recommended by Mr. Tom Moore, who, I believe, has the respect of all the labour people of Canada. I listened to the speech of one of our good friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party who specializes in labour problems. Everyone knows that he specializes so much that he spends a good deal of his time in travelling around Canada to meet and address labour people, which he has a right to do, I will admit. To my surprise, however, very often within a few weeks after he has left the labour people whom he addressed, labour trouble or strike followed in some instances. Let us read now what he said in his speech, as reported at page 3973 of Hansard:
I do not care what tag they give me-C.I.O., A.F. of L. or Canadian Congress of Labour.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I draw your attention to this. I quote:
John L. Lewis has taken us around by the ears so much that I do not know where we stand on these things.
Well, as a professional man, representing labour in the house and, I may say, representing one of the largest constituencies in Canada, I have done everything possible in the past to help labour, not only here, but in the legislative assembly of Quebec. May I add incidentally that I served free of charge as chairman of a board of conciliation which attempted to try to do something for labour.
But those of us who are not simply serving a party, but who wish to serve our country by serving labour will never say that we have been taken by the ears by John L. Lewis so often that we do not know where we stand. We believe in one thing-it is not the direction of John L. Lewis, or anybody else, especially if they come from outside the country-that will orient our conduct in Canada. Let me say to hon. members what I have said on many occasions to my many friends in the United States-and I have no hesitation in making this statement, and take full responsibility for it: I state, not as a member of parliament in Canada, but as a Canadian, that if we had John L. Lewis in Canada he would have been in a concentration camp a long time ago.
Canadians in general have much sympathy for labour. The people know, as I know, that
War Appropriation-Labour

labour has not received all that to which it is entitled. I know perfectly well that employers -not all, but certainly some of them-do not do what they should for their employees. So far as I am concerned, I am not interested in the racketeering alleged to take place in labour organizations. I believe it is time to protect labour first and, I will repeat what my hon. friend said, when speaking about order in council 2865-and I believe he was right-"that in veiy clear language the order in council gave the workers the right to organize."
I have had an opportunity of serving labour organizations, and of realizing how generous are the orders in council for the benefit of working men, but I realize, though, that there are no teeth in those orders in council, neither is there always a sanction. We have very generous labour laws, and we recognize the right of labour to organize. The law even punishes employers who do anything detrimental to the right of employees to organize. Provisions have been set up to appoint conciliation boards. But, I repeat, there are no teeth in these regulations; there is no sanction, and we cannot punish employers or employees if they do not follow the advice of the labour board.
May I make a suggestion to help the working man and the employer, so that we may have peace and order in our country? Is it not time that we oblige our labour unions to incorporate, in order that they may be responsible organizations? What do our labour organizations ask for? They ask for compulsory bargaining powers. And what is the meaning of that? Well, we ask employers and employees to sit at the same table, to discuss their problems, and come to an agreement. For instance, they may decide that they will take a vote in the plant to choose which labour organization will be the bargaining agent. After the bargaining agent is chosen, a man or a group of men will make a contract with the employer. Such contract would be made effective for one or two years. But what happens? Well, three or four months after the contract is made, another labour organization -the C.I.O., the A.F.ofL. or some such group -enter the plant and try to organize. They say, "We are the majority. This contract is no good. We will have to be chosen to replace the former collective bargaining agent, and another contract will have to be drawn up." After all, a contract is a contract. We are fighting this war because we believe in the sanctity of contracts. What happens among individuals when a party fails to keep a contract? The party is prosecuted in the courts. An employer can be prosecuted because he is

a responsible party, but labour unions, not being incorporated, are not responsible and cannot be prosecuted. In saying that, I am thinking of my friends, the labour class, not only of my constituency, but of Montreal and elsewhere in Canada. They are honest people, and they believe in the sanctity of contracts. I believe the time has arrived when the labour unions should be made to incorporate themselves in order that they may be responsible for any trouble that may occur through a strike.
I have great respect for union organizations, but not so much for certain organizers. If labour unions were held responsible, I wonder if some of these organizers would call strikes so quickly when they knew that there might not be enough money in the bank to pay their salaries? If we do not want to have occur here what is happening elsewhere; if we want to protect the labour organizations and employees-I insist upon this-if we want to respect the rights of the employers and of honest capital; if we want to keep order in this country the Minister of Labour should ask the cabinet to put more teeth by sanction in the legislation already enacted.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a question of privilege. I have been misrepresented by the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Fauteux) who has just taken his seat. If the remarks which I made last night and which he has attempted to discuss this evening went over his head, that is not my responsibility. If he had read my statement as set out in Hansard when I was discussing jurisdictional disputes, he would not have placed upon it the construction he has to-night. I was attempting to point out to the Minister of Labour that it was immaterial to me what tag was hung on any particular union, be it C.I.O., A.F. of L. or Canadian Congress of Labour. I stated, as set out in Hansard, that the rank and file of the labour men across this country who are attempting to organize are all fighting for the same principle, the right to a means of livelihood. I made certain remarks about my international president for whom I have a lot of respect, and who is respected by everyone on the north American continent who has had any connection with labour in the last thirty years. I merely tried to amplify my position in connection with affiliation and to show my complete disregard for it. I was not particular about what centre my international president is affiliated with in the near future. I have been in the A.F. of L.; I have been in the C.I.O., and I am now a member of the Canadian Congress of Labour.

War Appropriation-Labour
I rise to a point of order. The hon. member has said that he has been misrepresented, but I quoted what was in Hansard.
The hon. member read what suited him. He pulled a couple of sentences out of the context to make it appear as though it read exactly what he was talking about.
I read what is contained in Hansard.

If anyone compares the lot of the workers who are led by John L. Lewis in the United States with the wages and conditions of the workers in Quebec, I think he will agree that it would be well for that province if they had a couple of John L. Lewises in the field of labour. To the best of my knowledge the only crime he has ever committed is to fight for the workers whom he represents and who pay him his wages.
He is even blamed by Russia.
That is rubbish.
He fights for the members who have elected him.
To lose the war.

He takes his instructions from the international convention. Wage agreements are drafted by the policy committee which is set up by the rank and file of the union. He has no alternative but to follow the instructions of the international convention unless he is released by that body.
He is no leader at all.
He is a democrat. He takes his instructions from the people. The policy is drafted by the convention.
That is democracy.

If the hon. member for St. Mary is trying to create the impression that anyone in this country is pulling me around by the nose or by the ears, he is making a mistake. I was merely amplifying my complete disregard for any of these tags. Every'section of labour in Canada is fighting for the same principle as I am fighting for. The quicker we get away from all this busines of C.I.O., A.F. of L., Canadian Congress of Labour, Catholic syndicate and what have you, the quicker the problems faced by the Minister of Labour will be solved.
The hon. member stated that I travel a lot around this country. That is quite true, and I intend to continue doing so. This is
still a free country. He has stated that every time I appeared in Ontario, Quebec or somewhere else, immediately a strike took place. I want to say that that is absolutely wrong.
I did not say each time.
My hon. friend will find if he checks the record-[DOT]
It happened very often.

-that I have never attended a meeting in any province of Canada unless I was invited to do so by the people who were sponsoring the meeting. There is not a man in this country who can say that I ever advised the workers to go out on strike.
That is true, and we know it. The Minister of Labour knows it well.
Just the very reverse has been true and with very good reasons-a strike is an obsolete weapon.
I do not think any labour leader wants a strike.

No, there is not one. I am sorry I have had1 to occupy this time, Mr. Chairman, but I have no intention in this house or out of it of allowing anyone to rise in his place and make a statement of the kind * that was made about me to-night. I would advise the hon. member to get the German labour laws. I have them in my office and he can see them. The kind of organization he would set up is exactly the same kind of organization that Hitler has in Germany. That is exactly what my hon. friend is advocating.
That is it exactly.
And if that is the kind of labour organization he wants, I will give him the labour laws of Germany.

First, I want to join with the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. McKinnon) in what he said about conditions in the civil service here in Ottawa, and more especially among the lower paid employees, those in grade 1. I think it is a crime to have the civil servants of this country paid wages by the government of Canada that are not sufficient to maintain a decent standard of living. As was pointed out by the hon. member, only twenty-five eivil service girls in grade 1 have been able to take advantage of the accommodation afforded by the new hostel that is being built here because their salaries are not sufficient for them to avail themselves of that accommodation. Anyone who has lived in Ottawa

War Appropriation-Labour

knows-I do not think there can be any argument about this at all-that one cannot live here on sixty, sixty-five or seventy dollars a month. As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said, and I am in entire agreement with him, the dominion government at least should try to be a model employer and set an example in that respect.
I wish to say a word about the government's labour policy in general and then refer to a particular case or two. Working conditions in this country, generally speaking, are not good. I think we have had far too many strikes, perhaps not as many as other countries have had, but still we have had too many, and there has been too much disruption of work. I believe that every one of these strikes could have been averted if a proper investigation had been carried on beforehand and efforts had been made to iron out the difficulties.
Let us go back to the first of the war to show where the lack of planning came in. The Minister of Labour said, as reported at page 3940 of Hansard:
Hon. members should keep uppermost in mind the magnitude of our navy, army and air force and the fact that our industrial output and food production is now the greatest in our history.
That is well to remember. But that is the very thing the government did not remember. That is just where they fell down. I am not blaming the present minister for that, because he was not in office when the war started. When the war first started, that was the time our labour conditions should have received attention and when planning for the future should have been done. Anyone who had to do with administration or with labour would know that to raise an army, navy and air force and satisfy the needs of war industry would take a tremendous amount of careful planning, and that if you simply took men and women from all sources of employment and put them into the army, navy and air force in the numbers in which they were taken in, and in the manner in which they were allowed to come in, there was bound to be disruption. There was no planning there. Whether these young men were enlisted voluntarily or whether it was conscription, I am not going to argue at the present time.
On the next page of Hansard, page 3941, the Minister of Labour is reported to have said:
The commendable desire of our young men and women to volunteer for service in the navy, army and air force naturally led to shortages of labour for the jobs at home.
May I suggest to the minister that he has given the cause of the trouble right there in his own words when he said that these men and

women were enlisting in all the different branches of the armed services and were allowed to go anywhere. No wonder, there is now a great deal of difficulty in taking care of the needs of agriculture, of the coal mines, of war industry and of the armed services! We started out without any planning with respect to man-power. The minister went on to say :
These shortages have been added to by the thousands of men called up for service in Canada under the National Resources Mobilization Act. In addition to the drain of man-power into the armed services, the movement of men and women into war plants creates difficult problems with which we are dealing every day.
I am not blaming, the minister for making that statement, because it is true. But when he uses these words to try to give people the impression that everything is well and under control, he is missing the point entirely.
I'want to speak of the situation in our coal fields. I think the coal shortage is going to be one of our major problems. I have spoken of this before, but I mention it again because I see great danger ahead of us. The coal situation has become so serious that the government has declared a state of national emergency in fuel. There is no danger at the present time of a shortage of coal for domestic consumption. This is not the time of the year for that. But there may easily be a crisis as regards the supply of industrial coal. The users of industrial coal may not be able to get their supplies even at this time of the year, and if mining conditions get any worse in the United States we in Canada will be faced with a very serious problem indeed. It is no use just sitting down and hoping that the United States will settle their labour troubles and that our coal requirements will be taken care of by importations from the United States. It is high time that we should begin to develop a coal policy for Canada, to produce at least sufficient coal to take care of our own needs. We have an abundance of coal on both sides of this country, and there is no reason why we should be dependent upon the United States for coal for either industrial or domestic use. The strike in the coal mines in the United States is causing a great deal of fear in Canada, because we are now dependent upon the United States for our coal supply,.
The Minister of Labour said, as reported at page 3932 of Hansard:
Last October we arranged to have coal miners receive special consideration for postponement of military service and instructed national selective service officers not to issue any permits for coal miners to seek any other employment. Then we arranged to have coal miners granted leave from the armed services in Canada if they were willing to return to the mines. Subsequently we established the emergency coal production board after full consultation with

War Appropriation-Labour
the national selective service advisory board and the man-power advisory committee of the coal^ industry.
We have issued an order requiring all ex-coal miners to return to coal mining regardless of their present occupations and are guaranteeing them full employment. .
That is a big undertaking, guaranteeing them full employment. I hope the minister can fulfil it.
He speaks of soldiers getting out of the army. If he is depending upon that, I warn him now that it will not work as smoothly as he supposes. Only this week a man from the armed forces came into my office. He is a miner; I know him personally, and I know the mine from which he came; it also is in the Drumheller area. He has tried, since the minister made his statement on this matter, to get released from the armed forces, and he told me, "You cannot get near your commanding officer."

Perhaps the hon.
member will give me the man's name privately.

I went
this far:	I said, "When you return to your
camp, ask to go before your commanding officer; if you cannot get to him this time let me know, and I will personally take it up with the minister." But here is the difficulty: very few of these cases are likely to come either to the attention of private members or to the attention of the minister. The man told me that as soon as he managed to get by the sergeant and went to the major, he was pushed back with the remark, "We need you here, and you are not going to get out." There are not very many men in the army who will be so persistent as to keep on trying to get out, because there are lots of ways of discouraging miners in the army from not pressing too hard to be released in order to return to the mines. Therefore I say that if the minister is expecting to get many miners from the armed services back into the mines in order to settle a national emergency, I fear he is due for a disappointment. If there is a national emergency such as the Prime Minister indicated, I am definitely of opinion that other measures will have to be taken either to get miners or to release those who are in the armed forces, because I see difficulties looming up at the present time.
I wish to bring one particular case to the minister's attention, and that is all I shall deal with this evening; anything else I have to say will be deferred until we are on the estimates under the different topics to which they refer. I believe a little more consideration should be given to the working man in
regard to his employment. Not all these strikes which are occurring are the fault of the miners. I wish to refer specifically to the strike which took place at Drumheller when seventeen mines were affected and over 2,000 miners ceased work. It lasted, I believe, for about two weeks, and thousands of tons were not produced on account of it. It is true that the strike was settled, but the problem which was facing the miners is not settled. Certainly it was not settled by the board which was appointed to arbitrate the case. Judge Tweedie, I believe, was the chairman and was appointed by the- dominion government. The difficulty in that case was a matter of principle, whether a mine operator could fire a miner at any time he wanted to, for almost any reason. It is true that the strike was settled, but only when another mine, the Red Deer Valley mine, hired the man who had been dismissed from the Star mine; that relieved the situation and these fellows went back to work. But I believe the same difficulty will arise again, and I wish to point out to the minister what I think was the very unfair attitude taken by the judge in rendering his decision with regard to this strike. The minister should take precautions that such a thing does not occur again. I happened to be in Drumheller at that time, and was talking to these fellows, some of whom I know personally, and they gave me some of the correspondence they had had. I should like to put it on record for the minister's information.
This is a copy of Mr. Justice T. M. Tweedie's ruling in the case of Mike Bokos, given by telegram. Bokos is the man who was fired and whose dismissal is supposed to have been the cause of the strike:
Re Bokos reemployment at Star mine. Bokos was a member of the local union of the United Mine Workers of America at Star mine and along with other members of the union -went out on an illegal strike in violation of wage agreement then in force between district No. 18 United Mine Workers of America and various coal companies operating in Drumheller and Wayne districts Alberta as a result of which the Star mine was shut down for two weeks in February last. Bokos thereby ceased to be an employee of the Rosedale Collieries Ltd. Star mine. The company refused to reemploy him. The company was within its rights in doing so. I do not recommend his reemployment.
Statements of fact in Judge Tweedie's ruling are obviously wrong.
In whose opinion?

The men right there on the ground. In the first place this states that Bokos, a member of the local union, along with other members of the union
4026
War Appropriation-Labour

went out on an illegal strike. That man was not even employed by the mining company when the strike was called. He was on compensation from the provincial government. He had been hurt in an accident in the mine a little while before, and was still out on compensation. That is one statement which is definitely wrong and can be so proven from the records. The telegram states that "Bokos thereby ceased to be an employee of the Rosedale Collieries." The reason given is not at all how the dispute arose. It happened that something like two months before, there had been a little dispute regarding this man in the overloading of a car. But it was never drawn to his attention, and he was not fired on that account; in fact he was not fired at all. This is a matter of principle with the miners in Drumheller. It was not that they particularly cared about an individual as such, but the case involved the principle of whether a mine owner could just deliberately fire a fellow whenever he wanted to. That is what the union were fighting about, and of course that is what a union is for.
I want to put another document on record for the minister's information. This is from Rosedale Collieries Limited, Rosedale Mine, Rosedale Mine Post Office, Alberta, dated April 13, 1943, and it was sent to Mr. William Briggs, secretary, sub-districts 1 and 2, district 18, United Mine Workers of America, Drumheller:
I wish to acknowledge your letter of April 8 together with enclosure of a copy of a letter addressed to the Drumheller Coal Operators' Association. The purpose of these communications is apparently to threaten a strike unless one. Mike Bokos, is hired by the Rosedale collieries at the Star mine.
The employment of the above person was one of the disputes referred to Judge Tweedie as an independent chairman appointed by the dominion government. As Judge Tweedie has not as yet rendered his decisions on the matters in dispute, it would probably not be ethical that they be discussed. However, your letter implies drastic action to enforce the desire of some portion of your membership and credits Judge Tweedie with certain statements in regard to the employment of this man.
In order that your membership might have the benefit of some of Judge Tweedie's statements, I herewith relate a portion of the discussion at least.
It developed that Mike Bokos is a citizen of a country at war with Canada and our allies.
I want the committee to notice this:
The judge made the following comment:
"I have no sympathy with an alien who would earn his livelihood in this country for a period of some 13 years, during which a family was supported by sending money back from this . country to the country of his citizenship. If this country is good enough for a man to earn his living in, it is good enough for him to become a citizen of, and to bring his family to where he intends to earn his living."

We are pleased to note that, in the last paragraph of your letter to me, peaceful solution of any controversy is desired as being beneficial to both parties and the country' as a whole.
The reason for my writing this letter is that your delegates may have this information before them at the discussion which you state will take place April 14, and where a decision as to your future action will be taken.
The information was the previous paragraph which I have read and which was in quotations. Apparently one of the main reasons why the judge rendered the decision he did, and agreed that the mine should not rehire this man, was that the man was an alien. Whether he is an alien from a country with which we are at war, or whether he is not, does not, I submit, constitute a ground upon which to decide a strike. I think the minister will agree with me in that regard. It is not sound. I have no more sympathy than anybody else with the man who comes here and earns his living in this country and takes his earnings back, or sends them back, to the country from which he came, and I do not care whether it is a country with which we are at -war or not. But that is a matter of immigration. In that connection, I would say that if any man comes here and after remaining in the country for five years does not take out his naturalization papers he should be deported. I would not give him ten or fifteen years; I would reduce the period to five years. Certainly, however, that is not a sufficiently good ground upon which to base a decision in a matter of this kind, and to declare that because this man is an alien we should agree that the mine is right and the strikers are wrong.
There was a considerable degree of hard feeling over this question, and the only thing that settled the strike was the fact that one of the other coal mining companies came to the rescue. This company' gets along very well with its men and, so far as I know, there has never been any trouble in the Red Deer Valley mines. It seems to be one of the few companies that have the ability to cooperate with the miners in any sort of labour-management programme.
Who wrote that letter?
The letter was from Rosedale Collieries Limited, per J. F. Harvie. I believe that every one of these strikes could be solved if there were a proper relationship between labour and management.

Can the hon. member tell us what the relationship is that is so satisfactory in that colliery?
Mr. JOHNSTON 'Bow River) : In the Red Deer Valley mine?

Sugar Allotment
How do they look after their men?

I do not know the details. I do not know what sort of plan they work on, but I have bought coal from them-a good deal of it-and I know personally many of the men working there. I also know the management, and to my knowledge there has never been a serious dispute. But that is one of the very few mines about which that can be said. I do not believe there are any strikes that cannot be amicably settled if we go about it in the right way, but certainly the moment one of these men is fired in the Drumheller valley again under similar circumstances, there will be another strike, because the trouble has not been settled and they are certainly not in agreement with the decision rendered by the judge. And I do not blame them. I will be frank with the minister. When I read those letters I said to these fellows that in my opinion the reason given was not a basis upon which the judge could give the decision which he rendered. They were very much perturbed about it; they were anything but satisfied. I do not know whether we are supposed to criticize a judge or not, but I think that was a very poor decision to make. I suggest that the minister should pay a little more attention to these strikes. He is a labour man and has worked among labourers, and it would not be amiss in many cases if he went to the spot himself where he would be able to settle the matter. I have my doubts whether a judge is a man capable of rendering a decision in this type of dispute.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I know the hon. member realizes that he may not attack the judiciary either in committee or in the house.

Well, let me say that I have my doubts whether a man occupying such a position should be chairman of such a committee. I do not believe that such men are in a position to know the true relationship that exists between labour and management. Take a lawyer out of this house-*
Take them all out.
-or take any lawyer in the city of Ottawa, whether you give him a judgeship or not, and I could name many of them around here-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Order.

I say, take any member here who happens to be a lawyer and send him to Drumheller to settle a dispute
between labour and management, and he would not know anything about it. And definitely that was the situation here. So that, instead of appeasing these labourers; instead of settling the strike fairly, it was purely a one-sided affair. As I have pointed out, although the strike terminated it was not by reason of the decision handed down by the chairman but by reason of the good judgment of one of the operators in another company in hiring the man. As a result of actions such as I have described we have lost thousands of tons of coal at a time when the Prime Minister declares that there is a national emergency. If that is any way of solving our labour problems, then I am afraid we are heading straight for a real emergency, and when this winter comes it will be too late to start making plans to meet any national emergency. The government had better start now.
Progress reported.
